 Brazil’s Lula defies odds to clinch poll victory against Flavio Bolsonaro 







RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil (AFP) — Brazil’s leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback on Sunday as he clinched election victory against right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who trounced him in the first round.

With Lula’s victory, Brazil staved off a conservative wave that has seen numerous countries — such as Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru — all shift right, backed by US President Donald Trump.

The leftist icon, who turns 81 on Tuesday, defied all projections to win an unprecedented fourth term.

According to official results, he won 51.7 percent of the votes to 48.2 percent for Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, who had entered election day confident with his lead in the polls.

Since the first direct election following the end of Brazil’s dictatorship in 1989, no candidate who lost the first round had gone on to win the second.

Fireworks and vuvuzelas rang out in Rio de Janeiro, while thousands of people dressed in red, the color of Lula’s Workers’ Party, streamed into the streets of Sao Paulo to celebrate.

In a video posted to social media, the president appeared jumping for joy,wearing red, star-shaped glasses, at a hotel in Sao Paulo, where he is scheduled to speak to the press later.

Flavio Bolsonaro, who is in Brasilia, has yet to react.

In Cinelandia Square, in the heart of Rio, Lula’s supporters were moved to tears.

Julio Canelo, 42, a lawyer hailed a victory for “the entire democratic spectrum.”

“It was the result of the people mobilizing, in the streets and online,” he told AFP.

The left swung into action with massive rallies after the first-round defeat, declaring “Never Again Bolsonaro” and revamping a lacklustre social media strategy.

The abstention rate decreased from the first round, falling from 21 percent to 19 percent.

A bitter campaign marred by scandals and mudslinging laid bare the deep divisions that have remained in the country of over 200 million people over the past decade.

Lula heads into a fourth term with a country divided, with almost half of the nation having rejected him, desperate for change.

Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, pitched himself as more moderate and jovial than his father and managed to galvanize conservatives as well as less ideological voters fed up with crime, the high cost of living and a sense of stagnation.

“We’re in a deep hole, things are dire. People can barely afford to eat — buying meat is out of the question,” said Tereza Cristina Ramos, a 68-year-old retiree, who voted in Rio de Janeiro.

After a campaign marred by scandal and mud-slinging, Sunday’s vote plunged into chaos after a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extending voting by two hours, at the request of Lula who said buses had been pulled from circulation in various cities, barring citizens from voting.

– Lula rises again –

Lula’s re-election marks another remarkable comeback for the man who grew up dirt poor in the northeast, in a family of illiterate farmers.

He rose to the presidency as a working-class hero, taking office for the first time in 2003. He was re-elected in 2006.

Revered for social welfare programs that lifted millions out of poverty, Lula made a dramatic return to office in 2022 elections after a corruption scandal saw him jailed for over 18 months.

The charges, annulled on procedural grounds, have continued to haunt him.

In his third term he has overseen a drop in inflation and unemployment, and lifted millions out of hunger, but many voters who turned to Flavio Bolsonaro felt gloomy about their economic situation and fed up with crime.

After a campaign marked by fearmongering on both sides — many voters reported choosing what they considered the lesser evil.

– A tricky term ahead –

Already one of the world’s oldest leaders, Lula will be 85 by the end of his new term in 2030.

He will thus have spent 16 years in power, following his first stint as president from 2003 through 2010.

Lula is also facing a hostile Congress dominated by the right.

His options are constrained by the economic outlook, with growth expected to slow.

He has also come under renewed pressure to confront rampant security problems in a country plagued by criminal factions that sow terror in working-class neighborhoods.

The president’s campaign leaned heavily on the theme of sovereignty in the face of commercial and diplomatic pressure from Trump’s United States.

Voters must “choose a country where the flag is respected,” he said, his raspy voice more hoarse than ever after a tireless campaign. He accused his rival of wanting to “govern with the American flag.”

news.title: Bolsonaro calls for Brazil election results to be ‘annulled’ after loss to Lula
news.text:
Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of President Donald Trump, was reelected Sunday in a result that provides relief to critics of widening US influence in Latin America.

With 100 per cent of the vote counted, Brazil's electoral court announced that the soon to be 81-year-old Lula had a lead of nearly 4.4 million votes — 51.8 per cent of the total vote — over opponent Flávio Bolsonaro. The announcement capped an evening of chaos at polling places across Brazil, following a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours.

Late Sunday, Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat, calling the move to extend voting hours unprecedented — though both he and Lula made the request — and asked for the election results to be annulled, saying they were impossible to accept.

Lula's triumph bucks a trend in Latin America where increasing numbers of right-of-centre presidential candidates allied with Trump have been winning. Lula's victory leaves Mexico and Brazil, Latin America's two most populous nations, with left-of-centre leaders. It also positions Latin America's largest economy, with a GDP of USD 2.6 trillion per year, to remain independent of the US, despite the pressure of increased tariffs imposed by Trump.

Lula's win confirmed by electoral court

A video published by Lula's campaign shows the veteran leader celebrating with First Lady Rosângela da Silva and allies after his runoff victory was confirmed by Brazil's electoral court.

Wearing star-shaped red glasses, he kissed his wife. Hundreds of his supporters began gathering on São Paulo's main artery to celebrate the victory.

In Rio de Janeiro, cars beeped their horns and a woman dressed in red — the colour of Lula supporters — shouted “You lost! Cry harder!” to four men in yellow and green sipping beers, Bolsonaro's signature colors. A huge roar echoed in the street as the result was confirmed.

Rodrigo Valentim, a 51-year-old businessman and supporter of Bolsonaro, said that another Lula government would harm the economy. He pointed to financial markets' positive reaction to the result of the first round, when Bolsonaro bested Lula.

“I don't understand how people can vote for Lula,” he said. “The country is collapsing.”

Bolsonaro had yet to respond to Lula's apparent victory, which, if confirmed by electoral authorities, will give him his non-consecutive fourth term as president. The next term begins on Jan. 5, 2027.

Trump made the comments at a ‌political rally ‌in Port Huron, Michigan, ahead ​of ‌next ⁠week’s ​midterm elections.

Attributing recent unrest in France to immigration, Trump said he would welcome immigrants from some countries but not from Norway “because I didn’t get the Nobel Prize ... So I don’t want anybody from Norway.”

There ⁠was no indication that the ‌Trump administration was adopting ‌new official policy on Norwegian ​immigrants.

“Norway has become ‌a shit house country, actually,” Trump said, ‌using a term that he has previously applied to Haiti, Libya, Somalia and Yemen.

Norway is among the highest-income countries as measured by ‌GDP per capita, according to International Monetary Fund data. Norway’s sovereign wealth fund ⁠posted ⁠a record profit of 1.75 trillion Norwegian crowns ($184.3 billion) for the first half of 2026.

Norway’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and a representative for the Norwegian Nobel Committee did not immediately return requests for comment outside regular office hours.

Trump earlier this month called the failure to give him a Nobel Peace Prize an “indelible ​stain” on Norway.

news.title: Microsoft tells UK data centre developer ‘not possible’ as power supply delayed to 2030
news.text: Microsoft has withdrawn from a major UK data centre deal. The decision is a setback for British AI infrastructure developer Nscale, which had planned to make its Loughton, Essex, facility operational next year. The project has faced repeated delays, with electricity grid operators reportedly saying power won't be available until the 2030s. Microsoft had agreed to lease 23,000 Nvidia AI chips at the site and was expected to become its anchor tenant.​According to a report by The Telegraph, the withdrawal also comes as Nscale prepares for a potential US stock market listing that could value the company at up to $35 billion (£26 billion), raising questions about its expansion plans and investor confidence in AI infrastructure businesses.​Microsoft withdraws from Nscale's Essex data centre project​Microsoft recently informed Nscale that it was pulling out of the agreement announced last year. The deal was part of Microsoft's broader UK investment commitments worth £22 billion, announced during US President Donald Trump's visit to the country.​The proposed facility would have housed thousands of high-performance Nvidia AI chips. However, difficulties securing electricity connections have delayed the project, forcing Nscale to look for alternative energy sources and new expansion locations.​An Nscale spokesman said: “We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK, and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK. Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts.”​Microsoft did not comment on the decision.​Nscale's planned IPO faces fresh challenges​The setback comes as Nscale considers raising billions of dollars through a potential Wall Street listing. Backed by Nvidia and other investors, the company has been privately valued at $15 billion and reportedly targets a valuation of up to $35 billion through the proposed flotation.​Microsoft accounts for more than 40% of Nscale's $103 billion in contracted revenue, although the Essex project is believed to represent only a small portion of that amount. Anthropic is another major customer.​Long-term commitments from major technology companies matter for data centre developers, which need substantial financing to build facilities and buy computing hardware. Losing Microsoft's commitment to the Essex site could complicate Nscale's efforts to show it can deliver planned infrastructure projects.​Electricity shortages delay Britain's AI infrastructure plans​The Loughton case study highlights challenges in developing the country's AI infrastructure, including the high cost of electricity and long delays in grid connections.​Nscale has also encountered delays at a data centre project in Norway, reportedly resulting in significant penalties. Separately, OpenAI suspended plans in April for a Stargate AI facility with Nscale on Tyneside, citing Britain's high electricity prices.​The wider AI infrastructure sector has faced investor concerns over rising borrowing costs and whether demand will justify the substantial spending required to build data centres. Australian rival Firmus cancelled plans for a $20 billion IPO earlier this month, citing market conditions, while other infrastructure providers have also experienced pressure on their shares and bonds.​Nscale, founded by Australian entrepreneur Josh Payne two years ago, continues to pursue its UK expansion plans despite the Essex setback. The project's future will depend partly on whether the company can secure an alternative power supply and find another customer for the facility.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. news.title: Trump critic Lula wins reelection in Brazil, beats Bolsonaro to secure 4th presidential term
news.text:
Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of President Donald Trump, was reelected Sunday in a result that provides relief to critics of widening US influence in Latin America.

With 100 per cent of the vote counted, Brazil's electoral court announced that the soon to be 81-year-old Lula held an unassailable lead of nearly 4.4 million votes over opponent Flávio Bolsonaro.

The announcement capped an evening of chaos at polling places across Brazil, following a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours. That decision by a Supreme Court justice may trigger legal action by Bolsonaro.

His triumph bucks a trend in Latin America where increasing numbers of right-of-centre presidential candidates allied with Trump have been winning.

Lula's victory leaves Mexico and Brazil, Latin America's two most populous nations, with left-of-centre leaders. It also positions Latin America's largest economy, with a GDP of USD 2.6 trillion per year, to remain independent of the US, despite the pressure of increased tariffs imposed by Trump.

The announcement kicked off celebration by supporters inside and outside of the Sao Paulo hotel where Lula watched the count with First Lady Rosângela da Silva.

Lula's victory, if confirmed by electoral authorities, will give him his non-consecutive fourth term as president. The next term begins on Jan. 5, 2027.

It is the first time since Brazil's military dictatorship ended in 1985 that the second-highest vote-getter in the first-round elections won the presidency. Bolsonaro had 47 per cent of the vote in the first round to Lula's 45 per cent, a difference of 2.2 million votes.

Lula and Sen. Bolsonaro have yet to address their supporters.

Confusion at polling places

The electoral court's announcement ended an evening of confusion at polling places after Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ruled three minutes before the scheduled end of voting to keep polls open for two more hours, following requests by both candidates. Lula's request came after issues with buses that provide transportation to polls in Sao Paulo and Salvador, two cities that tend to favor the incumbent. Bolsonaro's request was due to heavy rains in Brazil's south, where he is favored.

In Brasilia, volunteers who oversaw the vote count at a school debated whether they needed to stay after the announcement to extend voting, but most left 15 to 20 minutes after polls closed and they had given count information to electoral authorities. At a polling station in Rio de Janeiro, the voting machines had already been switched off minutes after polls were set to close and couldn't be turned back on.

The decision delayed tallying the votes by two hours. It was unclear how many polling stations stayed open after the scheduled closing time.

Bolsonaro ally Nikolas Ferreira noted that Zanin, who made the decision, is Lula's former lawyer.

Security and cost-of-living concerns

Bolsonaro bested Lula by more than 2.2 million votes in the first round of the election earlier this month.

Lula faced a tough reelection battle because of concerns about the cost of living and security. Bolsonaro made a tough-on-crime approach the cornerstone of his campaign and pledged to bring down food costs while Lula, trying to lure undecided voters, has invested in costly incentives.

Both have been hit by corruption suspicions involving family members and allies, with Bolsonaro implicated in a sprawling scandal rocking Brazil. Lula previously spent more than a year in prison on corruption convictions that were eventually annulled.

Sunday's victory will likely be the last of the veteran leader's political career. Lula began his political career in the 1970s as a union leader. He then helped found the Workers' Party, which he represented as a presidential candidate three times until he finally won it in 2002. He was reelected four years later and was succeeded by one of his cabinet ministers, Dilma Rousseff, in 2010. She was reelected in 2014.

Rousseff was impeached for accounting maneuvering in 2016 amid a sprawling corruption probe, which also ensnared Lula. He tried to run for president again in 2018 but was jailed in March after being convicted.

Lula was released from prison after 580 days and saw Brazil's Supreme Court annul his sentence after police found messages that showed the judge who convicted him was biased. He quickly became one of former President Jair Bolsonaro's biggest critics and narrowly beat him in 2022.

Lula admitted in 2024, two years into the job, that his administration had done little thus far to earn the support of his voters.

Since he lost the first round, Lula reorganized his campaign, appealed to young voters, put millions of Brazilians on the streets to defend democratic values and his legacy, raised fears of another Bolsonaro administration and boosted several government initiatives.

Lula also defended Brazil's sovereignty and insisted that a Bolsonaro presidency would allow the US to exert control over Brazil.

He joins Trump and Nicaragua's President Daniel Ortega — all aged 80 — as the oldest presidents in the Americas. 

Published on October 26, 2026
news.summary: With 100 per cent of the vote counted, Brazil’s electoral court announced that the soon to be 81-year-old Lula held an unassailable lead of nearly 4.4 million votes over opponent Flávio Bolsonaro.

news.title: Trump Unloads on Bill Maher in 1,300-Word Post After White House Dinner
news.text: President Donald Trump launched a lengthy attack on comedian Bill Maher on Sunday, calling him a “complete and total loser” in a Truth Social post and telling him not to seek another meeting after previously hosting him twice at the White House. The 1,300-word broadside followed Maher’s discussion of his October 15 dinner with Trump during Friday’s episode of Real Time With Bill Maher, where he defended meeting with the president while continuing to criticize and joke about him. Maher has faced criticism over his willingness to engage with Trump despite their longstanding political differences, but has argued that speaking directly with the president is worthwhile. “I go and say face-to-face to the man the things you write in articles he’ll never read,” Maher said Friday on his HBO show. He also defiantly made clear that he enjoyed the experience, saying: “I like these dinners.” Maher has also spoken positively about his personal interactions with Trump, even as he has continued to criticize the president politically. Speaking with Trump's former press secretary Karoline Leavitt during Friday’s show, Maher said of Trump: “He looks you in the eye, he never interrupts, he never gets mad, he listens.” Trump also praised Leavitt’s appearance on Maher’s program, saying in his Truth Social post that she had defended both herself and the president “so well,” while accusing the show of treating her unfairly. Despite those warmer exchanges, Maher’s monologue also included a series of jokes and criticisms directed at Trump. He mocked the president’s approval ratings and recent comments about men’s physiques, while joking about his own return to the White House. “Trump has the lowest approval rating of any midterm candidate ever,” Maher said, before joking: “Only 1 percent of the Republicans are mentioning him in their ads.” He also said, “It’s just a little odd that Trump keeps gushing about men’s bodies, and how handsome they are, and their jawlines, and their asses, their physiques. I’m a little hurt. I was there for dinner for four hours last week, and not a peep. Nothing.” Maher said he raised several contentious subjects during the dinner, including immigration enforcement, Afghanistan, the Supreme Court and the 2020 presidential election. In his Sunday response, Trump sharply disputed Maher’s portrayal of both the dinner and his presidency. “Bill: Don’t call anymore. It’s useless,” Trump wrote, calling Maher a “hopeless guy” and “a coward” who was catering to his audience. Newsweek reached out to HBO for comment on behalf of Maher via email Sunday. Trump also disputed Maher’s claim that their latest dinner lasted four hours, saying it lasted “two hours, maybe less.” The president nevertheless described the gathering positively, writing that he thought it was a “good meeting” and that “everybody was happy.” The dinner also included musician Kid Rock and ESPN personality Stephen A. Smith. Trump had previously suggested that Maher liked him more privately than his public persona indicated, telling reporters after the gathering that the comedian “likes me a lot more than people understand.” Maher, meanwhile, has argued that people who disagree with the president should engage with him rather than avoid him. Earlier this month, on Maher's Club Random podcast, he said critics should tell Trump directly when they disagreed with his policies, adding: “He needs more people like us, not less.” The latest clash comes months after Maher received the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor at the Kennedy Center in March, adding another chapter to his complicated relationship with Trump. That tentative warming appears to have reached its limits on Sunday. Trump accused Maher of returning to his “old ways” after their meetings and criticized his comments on subjects ranging from Republican candidates and California voting to the administration’s policies toward Iran. Despite recounting their White House meetings at length, Trump ended his post by making clear he had little interest in another one. “You’re not transformative, you’re a Loser!” he wrote. news.title: Trump invokes 9/11 in urging Michigan voters to oppose Democratic Muslim Senate candidate El-Sayed
news.text:
PORT HURON, Michigan: President Donald Trump at ​a Sunday campaign rally ratcheted up his push to link US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed to Muslim extremists, comparing him to the 9/11 attackers while saying Democrats would let violent anti-American terrorists into the United States.

“I’m here to keep a jihadist, Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator,” the president told a receptive audience in Port Huron, which is in a Michigan area where 66 percent of the vote went to Trump in the 2024 presidential election.

If El-Sayed wins, he would be the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. Trump has sought to paint him as an anti-American Muslim radical, and on Sunday he took the rhetoric to a new level, likening El-Sayed to the attackers who took over United Flight 93 during the September 11, 2001, attacks.

El-Sayed has ‌dismissed the accusations ‌against him and, in a recent advertisement, defended his religion, saying, “Faith is a thing there’s ​just ‌too ⁠little of ​in ⁠Washington.”

Michigan has one of the nation’s most competitive US Senate contests going into the November 3 midterm elections, with former US Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican, and El-Sayed vying for an open seat that will help to decide control of the chamber.

The president on Sunday compared voting against El-Sayed to the actions of Michigan native Todd Beamer and others who fought back against the Flight 93 hijackers.

“Twenty-five years later, Michigan needs to stand up and fight, just like Todd did, to stop a jihadist from walking into the Capitol,” Trump said.

El-Sayed says questioning his loyalty is ‘shameful’

The mostly White crowd at Sunday’s rally cheered Trump’s comments on El-Sayed. Some attendees yelled “traitor” and others yelled “deport,” although El-Sayed ⁠was born in Michigan.

Terrance Camburn, a 52-year-old disabled Army veteran from Sandusky, Michigan, said he ‌supported Trump’s criticism because of El-Sayed’s “political beliefs.”

“I’ve been down to Dearborn and I’ve seen ‌many of the things he agrees with,” Camburn said when asked about Trump’s ​9/11 comments.

Dearborn, Michigan, has the highest per-capita concentration of Muslims of ‌any US city.

As he left the venue after the rally, Rogers did not respond to Reuters’ questions about Trump’s invocation ‌of 9/11. But earlier on Sunday, he said on NBC’s “Meet the Press” that he did not agree with the notion that El-Sayed is a violent terrorist.

“I’ve never called him a terrorist,” Rogers told NBC.

Rogers has alleged without evidence that El-Sayed has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world’s oldest and most influential Islamist groups.

El-Sayed has denied affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood, saying it is “shameful” for Rogers to question his ‌allegiance to the United States.

Rogers told “Meet the Press” that El-Sayed had not sufficiently responded to questions about the allegations.

Trump’s speech in eastern Michigan on Sunday came a day after former President Barack Obama campaigned for Democrats in the state, underscoring its importance in next week’s elections.

At a Saturday rally in Detroit, Obama framed the attacks by El-Sayed’s opponents as an attempt to make him look “less American than they are.”

The former president compared them to his experience as the target of false claims that he was born in Kenya.

“We have seen this movie before,” Obama said. “I starred in it ... This stuff didn’t work on me. Not in Michigan. It’s not going to work on Abdul.”

Manufacturing investments

“There’s some good and there’s some things we have to work on,” he told “Meet the Press.”

Trump ​praised Rogers during Sunday’s rally as a “perfect” candidate. “He’s like central ​casting,” Trump said.

Democrats need to gain just a handful of seats each in the US Senate and House of Representatives to overturn Republicans’ narrow 53-47 and 218-214 majorities.

news.title: Lula beats Bolsonaro in Brazil election to win unprecedented fourth term
news.text: Brazil's incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has beaten his rival to win an unprecedented fourth term. With 100% of the vote counted, Brazil's electoral court has announced. Lula's win follows a chaotic evening at the polls , where a last-minute decision was made to extend voting by two hours. The win also comes as a Supreme Court justice said the change may trigger legal action by Bolsonaro . Just three minutes before the vote, Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ruled to keep polls open for two more hours, following requests by both candidates . A Bolsonaro ally noted that Zanin is Lula's former lawyer. Lula's request came after issues with buses that provide transportation to polls in Sao Paulo and Salvador, two cities that tend to favour the incumbent. Bolsonaro's request was due to heavy rains in Brazil's south, where he is favoured. The 80-year-old leader is a vocal critic of US President Donald Trump and his win bucks a trend in Latin America where increasing numbers of right-of-center presidential candidates allied with the American leader have been winning. Lula's win comes after a tough re-election battle over concerns about the cost of living and security. He began his political career in the 1970s as a union leader. He then helped found the Workers' Party, which he represented as a presidential candidate three times until he finally won it in 2002. He was re-elected four years later and was succeeded by one of his cabinet ministers, Dilma Rousseff, in 2010. She was re-elected in 2014. Sunday's victory will likely be the last of the veteran leader's political career. The announcement was followed by celebration by Lula's supporters inside and outside of the Sao Paulo hotel where he watched the count with First Lady Rosângela da Silva. It is the first time since Brazil's military dictatorship ended in 1985 that the second-highest vote-getter in the first-round elections won the presidency. Bolsonaro secured 47% of the vote in the first round compared to Lula's 45% - a difference of 2.2 million votes. Lula will turn 81 on Tuesday.

news.title: Lula, Brazil’s iconic working class president, wins historic fourth term in dramatic comeback
news.text:
SAO PAULO — Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won an unprecedented fourth term on Sunday, the country’s electoral court said, in a shock result that defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America.

Lula, an icon of the global left and the most dominant force in Brazilian politics this century, defeated Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. The senator had finished first in the election’s first round and hoped to revive his father’s far-right movement.

At times, Lula’s reelection looked like a long shot, as voters soured on him and his Workers’ Party after years of corruption scandals and rising prices, while sweeping societal changes left the former metalworker and union leader looking out of touch with an increasingly app-based economy and its growing ranks of informal workers.

Lula’s victory marks another comeback in a career full of them. The 80-year-old was jailed from 2018 to 2019 on corruption charges that were later overturned, paving the way for him to beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election.

“He is a statesman, a giant,” leftist federal lawmaker Erika Hilton, who was with Lula in Sao Paulo during the vote count, told Reuters.

UNLIKELY PATH TO VICTORY
Pollsters said better-than-expected turnout had powered Lula to victory. Leonardo Barreto, the co-founder of consultancy Think Policy, said voters had chosen Lula’s familiar embrace over Mr. Bolsonaro’s novelty.

“People today are choosing between change, with some apprehension, and a known path, which guarantees certain rights,” he said.

During the campaign, Lula pointed to a track record of falling poverty and inequality, while unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation hit record lows during his third term.

He warned Mr. Bolsonaro would cut welfare spending, backslide on social advances and hand over Brazil’s sovereignty to US President Donald Trump, whose State Department led a campaign to get the Bolsonaros back to power.

Lula’s win deprives Mr. Trump of a major addition to what has been a growing bloc of friendly right-wing Latin American governments that have embraced Washington’s agenda on security and migration.

Celso Amorim, a former Lula foreign minister, told Reuters the leftist “would be very important for establishing a point of balance in Latin America. Lula is that balance.”

COMEBACK KING
Lula becomes the first candidate since Brazil’s return to democracy in the 1980s to be elected after finishing second in the first round.

Lula, who was president between 2003 and 2011, campaigned on a potent mix of pragmatism and populism that has shaped his career in national politics for half a century, rolling out a slew of reforms aimed at improving the lives of workers and poor Brazilians.

These gained steam with late-campaign pledges that ranged from free nationwide weekend public ​transport, which has to be formally submitted to Congress, to a ‌15% increase in his trademark welfare program that is already being implemented.

Lula also championed a constitutional amendment that became Brazil’s biggest labor reform in decades, which passed with wide support in Congress.

CHALLENGING LEGISLATIVE REALITY
Still, Lula’s fourth term could be his most difficult yet, after Brazil elected its most conservative Congress since returning to democracy in the 1980s.

Combined, Mr. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) and allied parties could control over 280 seats in the lower house and up to 50 seats in the Senate, enough for comfortable majorities in both chambers.

“He is likely to be a lame duck from the start,” said Oliver Stuenkel, a professor of international relations at the Getulio Vargas Foundation in São Paulo.

The incoming legislature will likely deepen recent trends of presidents ceding power to Congress, Mr. Stuenkel said, predicting Lula will face waning influence over Supreme Court nominations, unwieldy party coalitions, and even the threat of impeachment.

ECONOMIC HEADWINDS
Lula faces an economy that his government forecasts will grow a meager 2.3% next year, adding to fiscal concerns tied to high interest rates and public debt that has risen past 82% of GDP, the highest since the pandemic.

The president’s critics blame spending, though interest costs have driven most of the increase in debt.

Goldman Sachs said it expects Lula to make modest progress at most to contain spending in a fourth term, as he stays committed to a state-led growth model.

Surging household debt also concerns economists. Trying to address the issue, Lula rolled out a provisional ban on online betting and unveiled a new debt relief program during the campaign.

The incoming right-wing Congress will try to pass structural reforms that favor businesses, experts say, prompting spending cuts that could fuel social upheaval. — Reuters

news.text:
Tuesday’s election in Israel represents a crucial juncture for the Middle East, with Netanyahu’s right-wing government facing potential defeat. His removal from office would trigger a reset of the conflicts in Iran and Gaza and redraw the relationship between Jerusalem and US President Donald Trump.

Netanyahu – Israel’s longest serving prime minister and the country’s first sitting leader to be charged with a crime – has repeatedly invoked the security situation in the Middle East to argue for delays in giving evidence at his corruption trial.

Known as Case 1000, Netanyahu was in 2019 indicted on fraud and breach of trust charges for accepting luxury gifts from Packer and film producer Arnon Milchan worth about $295,000. Netanyahu is also accused of intervening on behalf of Milchan for various business matters, including a US visa renewal.

The 77-year-old prime minister completed his evidence on these charges and other unrelated allegations in July. The court is yet to deliver a verdict.

news.title: The unlikely role model in endless Donald Trump, Gavin Newsom beef
news.text:
Somehow Zohran Mamdani can meet with President Donald Trump, but Gavin Newsom can’t — or won’t.

Newsom’s office continues to make excuses for the governor’s refusal to work with the White House. 

In Newsom’s telling, it’s all Trump’s fault.

He tried to sell that story this weekend, after former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt told Bill Maher that Newsom and LA Mayor Karen Bass should give the president a call.

In Bass’s defense, she was once very hostile to Trump, but the mayor traveled to meet with him in April to discuss federal aid for rebuilding after the LA wildfires.

But Newsom has made a point of attacking Trump, often in obscene terms, on social media.

Newsom’s office claimed that the governor met with Trump for a full 90 minutes in February 2025, but then the president tried to order the National Guard to California to fight crime, over the governor’s wishes.

What that leaves out is the fact that Newsom signed a law in January 2025 authorizing $50 million in new funding to fight the Trump administration in court.

Half of that money was set aside to defend illegal migrants. The other half was to file broader lawsuits against the administration.

Newsom has said that the money was well spent, because it defended state interests, such as the continued flow of federal funding that the White House tried to block.

But there are other cases in which Newsom has tried to challenge national policies that have little to do with California — such as the firing of certain federal employees. 

The courts rightly threw out that case for lack of standing. But the damage that Newsom did to the state’s relationship with the White House continued.

Newsom also continued his profane rants against Trump, which bombed once he took his act overseas.

No one in Davos, for example, understood why the governor was selling kneepads on his website to mock Trump. When they didn’t laugh, he said he “should have brought a bunch of kneepads for all the world leaders.”

The least the American people can expect from elected leaders is that they work with one another. 

If Mamdani — a socialist who campaigns against the president — can play nice with Trump, then Newsom can do the same.

Instead, he chose to insult Trump, hoping to impress Democratic presidential primary voters.

It isn’t working. All Newsom did was hurt California.

news.title: Venezuela opposition leader Machado returns home after fraught year away
news.text:
CARACAS/BARQUISIMETO — Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returned home on Sunday after nearly a year away, following several failed attempts to return that strained her ties with US President Donald Trump’s administration.

“I’m here. With you all,” the Nobel Peace Prize winner wrote on X.

She appeared at a church in western Lara state, according to images shared by her press team, and was greeted by bystanders who sang the national anthem and shouted “liberty!” as she left in an SUV, a Reuters witness said.

Throughout the day on Sunday, she traveled toward Caracas by road as supporters gathered along her route to cheer her on.

Her return was coordinated with the US, Panamanian and Colombian governments, according to a person briefed directly on Ms. Machado’s movements and plans, who added that Mr. Trump approved her return and was kept informed about it.

At the White House on Sunday, however, Mr. Trump said he did not know anything about Ms. Machado’s return and suggested the US would continue to back Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez.

“She’s a very nice woman,” he said, referring to Ms. Machado. “But we’re doing really well in Venezuela.”

The White House and the State Department did not respond to Reuters questions on the matter.

MACHADO’S RETURN PREVIOUSLY DELAYED AT US REQUEST
Ms. Machado’s efforts to return have tested her relationship with the Trump administration, which she has sought to cultivate as an ally since before it removed former President Nicolas Maduro from power in January.

Mr. Trump has repeatedly expressed support for Ms. Rodriguez, a former deputy to Mr. Maduro, and hailed deals on oil production and other business ventures by US companies in the South American country. Mr. Trump said in September it was too soon to consider democratic elections in Venezuela.

US officials have asked Ms. Machado at least once to delay her return, Reuters reported in June, and she has made several failed attempts to enter the country. Her team did not disclose details of how she returned.

Ms. Machado traveled in a private plane from Panama to Colombia and crossed overland on Sunday to Venezuela, four people familiar with her movements told Reuters.

The person briefed directly on her movements said the flight took place late last week and she was guarded by US security contractors during her journey. Ms. Rodriguez and the country’s authorities were warned by the US not to interfere or threaten her safety, the person said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement on Sunday, “The conditions allowing for the safe return of Ms. Machado to Venezuela are the direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks which have already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile.

“We expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in thirty years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election but an enduring democracy.”

A faction of the opposition and the interim government held a round of talks this month, with the aim of remaking the top court and electoral council, among other goals, ahead of eventual elections. The talks have not included Ms. Machado’s political movement.

The Venezuelan Communications Ministry, which handles all press queries for the government, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Ms. Machado’s return.

SUPPORTERS CHEER MACHADO ON ROUTE TO CARACAS
As Ms. Machado traveled towards the capital on Sunday, thousands of people thronged to the side of the highway, many shouting, “María, we love you,” “welcome” and “freedom.”

“Maria Corina Machado will achieve liberty and democracy in Venezuela,” said Hernan Adames, 69, as he celebrated with other supporters in Barquisimeto.

Zuleima Granadillo, 61, an employee at the Ministry of Education, waited for Ms. Machado at a point along the highway in Aragua state, closer to Caracas.

“What does Machado’s arrival mean? All paths are opening up for us, the future is opening up, we have a light, and we are going all the way to the end,” she said.

“This dictatorship is already over with the arrival of our leader.”

Ms. Machado plans to meet with victims of the deadly earthquakes that struck Venezuela in June, as well as the families of political prisoners, the international community and various leaders from the democratic movement in Venezuela, David Smolansky, her top foreign affairs adviser, told Reuters.

“She will work proactively for a date for free and fair elections,” he added.

International energy firms committed last month to expanding projects in the country in a signing ceremony overseen by Ms. Rodriguez and US Energy Secretary Chris Wright.

Ms. Machado has said that only a “serious, democratic government” can provide the stability needed by investors.

She had been barred by Mr. Maduro’s government from exiting Venezuela but she secretly left in late 2025 to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, after spending more than a year living mostly in hiding.

Ms. Machado’s Vente Venezuela movement debuted an app on Saturday to ‌collect voter registration information from Venezuelans abroad. The group hopes eventually to share data from the app, which was built by 15 staff over the last 18 months, with a reformed electoral council so users can be officially added to voter rolls.

Edmundo Gonzalez, a former presidential candidate for Ms. Machado’s movement who has been living in Spain, said on X he would soon join her in Venezuela. — Reuters

news.title: The logic behind Trump’s ‘pretend I’m on the ballot’ appeal
news.text:
The answer is low-propensity voters. There are a lot of Republican-leaning voters in the 4th District of Iowa who don’t go to the polls for every election, but turned out in 2024 to vote for Donald Trump. They are the kind who probably wouldn’t turn out for a midterm election in 2026 with no Trump on the ballot. The GOP challenge is how to get their votes this time.

“MAGA low-propensity voters are a sizable part of our low-propensity voters,” Jeff Kaufmann, the longtime chairman of the Iowa Republican Party, told me. “There is no way to turn them out without Trump himself. They don’t get out to vote when Trump is not on the ballot.”

Kaufmann asked the president to visit those voters where they live. “I said to the president, there is no mailer, no commercial, that can turn out the MAGA portion of our low-propensity voters,” Kaufmann recalled. Only Trump in person.

Iowa Republicans know this because appealing to low-propensity voters is how they’ve won elections before. “They literally carried our current governor [Republican Kim Reynolds] over the line,” Kaufmann said. “She will tell you that her reelection was because of the 4th District. We don’t win statewide races, not just governor and Senate but attorney general and state auditor, without turnout in the 4th District — especially during a midterm.”

It’s not just in Iowa. On Friday, Trump traveled to Fort Myers, Florida, in a district he won by 31 points. On Saturday, he traveled to Perry, Georgia, in a district he also won by 31 points. And on Sunday, he traveled to Port Huron, Michigan, in a district he won by 32 points.

It’s not that Republicans are in trouble in those places. Far from it. It’s that Trump is aggressively trying to attract the voters who only come out when he is on the ballot — by asking them to vote like he is.

Trump has been widely mocked for asking voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot.” The New Yorker said it shows that “only one subject truly animates Donald Trump on the campaign trail, and it is, of course…himself.” The Daily Beast called it a “desperate plea.” And at his rally in Detroit Saturday with former President Barack Obama, Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul el Sayed ridiculed Trump’s visit to Port Huron and sarcastically asked voters, “Please make sure to vote like Donald Trump is on the ballot.”

Despite what he said, it’s probably safe to assume el Sayed does not really want the 9th Congressional District of Michigan, which includes Port Huron, to vote like Trump is on the ballot, since voters there gave the president that 32-point victory in 2024.

There is research showing that a low-propensity voter strategy makes sense in a lot of places. A 2025 report from Pew Research found that nationwide, voters who were eligible to vote in 2020 and 2022 but did not vote, and then did vote in 2024 — those voters leaned strongly toward Trump. He won the 2024-only voters by 55% to Kamala Harris’s 41%. And this was not just a tiny group of people. Pew found that 2024-only voters made up 12% of the entire electorate in the presidential race that year. It made a big difference for Trump.

Now the president is trying to do the same thing in the context of a midterm election. And if Republicans are trying to turn out low-propensity voters, it makes sense to ask them to pretend that Trump is on the ballot. It might not work, or it might not work everywhere. But it is probably the Republican Party’s best shot at the moment. Speaking the day after the Sioux City rally, Jeff Kaufmann said, “I think we accomplished our goal, which was to energize turnout in the 4th District.”

news.title: Season of protests
news.text:
A WAVE of protests is sweeping across the world in a season of unrest. From West to East, the street is confronting the state. Led predominantly by students and young people, protests have been widening to encompass other disaffected groups in society. In some cases, they are morphing into a nationwide movement. On almost every continent, governments are being put on notice that there will be a price to pay for misgovernance and being indifferent to public demands.

India’s Gen Z has been in the streets in anti-government protests against the controversial revision of electoral rolls. Students in France began protesting against deteriorating school conditions with other groups, including trade unions, joining demonstrations over high living costs and inequality. In Italy, students, farmers and truckers took to the streets in protests driven by education costs, economic grievances, and anti-war sentiment. In Brussels, students marched over education funding. Spain saw protests over a housing crisis. In Albania, student-led demonstrations occurred over living costs and a controversial tourism project linked to Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law. In Portugal, protests erupted over housing and falling living standards. There were education protests across Greece. In Brazil, thousands joined a student march against the election bid of far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro. Tunisia’s capital witnessed protests demanding the president’s resignation and democratic rights.

The triggers vary, as do the underlying causes. Each protest is rooted in its own political context. But there are common themes. All reject the status quo and indicate disenchantment with traditional political parties. All voice anger against unresponsive governments and the state failing them on their socioeconomic demands. The context for most protests is a cost-of-living crisis and deterioration or cuts in public services compounded by the state’s inability to deliver on education and jobs. Economic grievances and resentment of inequality are a driving force of the protests. A sense of disenfranchisement is another common thread. The heavy-handed response by governments to the protests and draconian crackdowns further fuelled the unrest and sparked violent clashes in several places. But it energised demonstrators to keep returning to the street. Unfortunately, in France protests degenerated into looting and rioting.

Protests in Europe and India share a defining feature. They are propelled by a wave of student activism. At their core is youth frustration in a generation that sees broken promises and an uncertain future. It feels betrayed by the lack of educational and economic opportunities. Protes-ters have also been venting rage against political leaders who have ignored public needs and are seen as venal. Initiated by young people, protests have expanded into broader movements as other disaffected groups, with their own set of demands, joined the demonstrations. Social media has been a key mobilisation tool in all the protests.

 Governments have been put on notice that misrule and ignoring public needs will have consequences.

None of the protests or movements have been party-led. Political parties have largely been sidelined, even as they tried to leverage the demonstrations; France’s left aligned itself with the protesters. In several European countries, protests are playing out in an environment of deep polarisation, which parties of both the left and right are trying to exploit. This is especially because elections are due next year in many countries including France, Spain, and Italy.

In India, the youth ‘Cockroach’ movement has spearheaded the protests and mounted the most significant challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government so far. The ongoing protests came against the backdrop of student protests led by the Cockroach party over the leak of exam papers in May, which forced the resignation of the education minister. This time, the catalyst was the revision of voter lists by India’s election commission, which apparently involved the removal of around 130 million voters. 

The government and the election commission’s claim that this was aimed at eliminating duplicate and ineligible entries was widely rejected. It was instead seen as a step towards mass disenfranchisement. It became the trigger for youth protests, demanding the resignation of the chief election commissioner and scrapping the revision. India’s opposition parties also joined the demonstrations and decried the move as a politically motivated purge to benefit the ruling BJP.

The Cockroach Janta Party used the opportunity to broaden its campaign. The government’s strong-arm tactics to suppress the popular upsurge only inflamed the demonstrators who accused Modi of “stealing democracy”. While these protests did not pose an existential threat to Modi, his jittery and increasingly autocratic government behaved as if they did — with arrests and a harsh clampdown. The scale of the protests and the government’s repressive response eroded Modi’s authority, weakened his grip on power, and dented his credibility and image.

The mass protests signified much more than opposition to the voter roll overhaul. They have been about democratic rights and democratic ac--c-o--untability and against pervasive injustice. As Indian academic Sudhir Kumar Suthar has arg-ued, they have been driven by the quest for dignity as much as for rights. The message from the young is clear: “they deserve a more dignified life than what they have received from the system so far.”

The central question is what will be the outcome of mass protests and what will they achieve? A definitive assessment has to wait until the protests play themselves out as most are still unfolding. But one unintended consequence of the current wave of discontent in some European countries, especially France but to a degree also in Spain and Portugal, may be to strengthen the far-right. The far-right has led none of these protests but it stands to benefit from their fallout. 

In a political landscape where the political centre is being hollowed out and centrist parties have lost touch with young people, unrest advantages the most organised opposition force that promises order. In France, that force is Marine Le Pen’s Rassemblement National. Where the hard-right is in power the advantage works differently. It enables governments to cast the protests as a law-and-order issue fuelled by migrants to justify harsher measures.

More generally, youth-led protests may force governments to take more seriously the needs and aspirations of young people which have rarely been a priority. What the streets are signalling is a breakdown of trust that can no longer be brushed aside. For now, the protests have put governments on notice: misrule has consequences. 

The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.

news.title: Lula wins fourth term as Brazilian President in runoff
news.text: Digital Desk | Brasilia, Oct 26 (IANS) Brazilian incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, candidate of the ruling Workers' Party, won Sunday's presidential runoff, according to results released by Brazil's Superior Electoral Court. With 99.89 per cent of the votes counted, Lula received 51.78 per cent of the valid votes, compared with 48.23 per cent for Flavio Bolsonaro, the Liberal Party's presidential candidate and son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, according to the official tally pulling off a remarkable comeback after trailing in the first round. Lula will be sworn in on January 5, 2027, for a four-year term, marking his fourth election as Brazil's president. He had trailed in the first round, blocking a rightward shift in Latin America that US President Donald Trump has backed. Lula is set to govern from 2027 to 2030, facing a Congress where Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party has held the largest bench in decades, and a public debt he must stabilise. Earlier on Sunday, taking to social media platform X, Lula said: “Once again, it was the Brazilian people who showed me that no dream is too big when we walk together. They were tireless days. Every walk, every act, and every march were much more than campaign moments. They were encounters of dreams that turned into concrete achievements, like the end of the 6x1 workday. Every outstretched hand and every smile reminded me why I dedicated my life to the fight for the workers of this country.” He further said: “We emerged from this journey stronger, more united, and more mobilised to ensure a better future. Thank you, Brazil, for every hug, every tear, every smile, and for never letting go of my hand. Our story still has many beautiful pages left to write.” In the first round of voting held on October 4, Bolsonaro led with 47.03 per cent of the valid ballots, narrowly surpassing Lula, who secured 45.16 per cent. This result set up three weeks of vigorous campaigning throughout Latin America's largest nation.

news.text:
Leak before the fix

The flaws were in PHP, a programming language estimated to run on some 70pc of the web. They had been found using AI tools, through a months-long effort coordinated by OpenAI. Under the long-standing practice of coordinated disclosure, details were meant to stay private until a fix was ready. On Wednesday, though, cybersecurity firm Chainguard released the information early. Its CEO Dan Lorenc later apologised, but argued the flaw was already being exploited, a claim others disputed. The early release set off a 72-hour scramble. Cyber agencies in Europe, the US, the UK, Australia and Canada issued urgent warnings, and several governments took websites offline as a precaution. Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince said the company had seen millions of attempts to exploit the flaw, up from thousands in the 10 hours before it was announced. Amazon’s cloud division also said it was being widely exploited. No major damage was immediately apparent, and Germany’s cyber agency said it had seen no successful attacks. But OpenAI warned that similar findings would rise sharply in the coming months. For now, agencies are urging organisations to install the fix released by the PHP Foundation. The head of the Dutch cyber agency summed it up as “patch, patch, and patch.” 

(Adapted from ‘Inside the cyber flaw scramble that brought the AI threat to life’, by Sam Clark, published on October 24, 2026 by POLITICO)

A gift you can’t refuse

Elon Musk said on October 19 that he would give one SpaceX share to every child in America, a gift worth $10.66 billion. President Donald Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have indicated the shares will go into Trump accounts, tax-advantaged investment accounts that now cover close to 70 million American children. The gift comes with strings. Account holders may have to keep donated shares for five years, or until the end of the year the child turns 17 if that comes sooner. In most cases they cannot sell, even if the price falls. Families also cannot choose or turn down stocks like SpaceX, and cannot leave the programme once enrolled. Donors may gain too. Giving through a vehicle such as a foundation can bring charitable tax deductions. 

--Adapted from ‘Elon Musk’s $10.5B SpaceX gift to kids has a catch: Families can’t refuse it — and may need to wait 5 years to cash out’, by Becky Robertson, published on October 22, 2026 by Moneywise/Yahoo Finance

Hi-tech park, low on gas 

When Bangladesh opened its hi-tech park in Sylhet in December 2021, the 171-acre site was meant to industrialise the region, create jobs for young people and tap markets in India’s seven northeastern states. Nearly five years later, the park has created around 400 jobs against a target of 20,000. It has drawn about $24.25 million in investment, a fraction of the $121.38m it was meant to attract. Only two of the 14 companies allotted land or space at the park are operational. Investors point to gas shortages, frequent power cuts and promised incentives that never arrived, such as one-stop government services and rent-free construction periods. Rangs Electronics, the park’s flagship tenant, has been unable to secure an industrial gas connection since applying in 2022. It is running at just 30 per cent of capacity.

Adapted from ‘Five years on, Bangladesh’s Sylhet hi-tech park struggles to take off’, by Dwaipayan Barua, published on October 22, 2026 by The Daily Star/Asia News Network

Beauty Boost

Popular weight-loss drugs like Ozempic, Wegovy, and Mounjaro are driving new trends in skincare. Because rapid weight loss often causes loose, sagging skin, beauty giant L’Oréal is seizing the opportunity. Chief Executive Nicolas Hieronimus highlighted this shift, noting that brands like SkinCeuticals and Kiehl’s offer products to counter these effects. Furthermore, L’Oréal holds a 20pc stake in dermatology firm Galderma. Both companies are now conducting clinical trials on GLP-1 users, following surveys showing noticeable facial changes among patients.

The flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz has returned to something close to pre-war levels. So why has the price surged again to near six-month highs?After trading below $US100 a barrel last month, the price climbed to just under $US117 a barrel last week, with pricing in the futures market suggesting it could still be trading above $US100 a barrel well into next year.With the elections just over a week away, Trump’s rhetoric has hardened.AP Photo/Alex BrandonThat’s despite shipments from the Middle East running close to their pre-war levels as the volume of oil mon tankers being escorted through the strait by the US navy – and some tankers that appear to be paying Iranian fees for safe passage – have rebounded.Flows through Saudi Arabia’s pipeline to the Red Sea have also picked up, despite Houthi attacks on the pipeline and the port of Yanbu.

The flows are holding up despite recent escalation of Iranian attacks on ships in the strait and Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure, oil fields and the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.Last week the UK’s Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) reported 11 confirmed attacks in the strait last week, although the real number is probably higher, given that the UKMTO says most targeted ships don’t report the attacks. Other authorities claim there have been at least 28 incidents so far this month.If the oil is flowing, why has the price taken off again?Part of the explanation may be that while more oil might be reaching the global market, the cost of getting it there has exploded.

Advertisement

The cost of chartering a tanker to carry oil through the strait is about 12 times what it was pre-war; the cost of insuring the cargo more than three times what it was.Ships captains are being paid nearly six times what they were being paid, plus bonuses in the tens of thousands of dollars, and crews two or three times their pre-war salaries, as incentives for taking the risk of being attacked.The way oil is being moved out of the strait – vessels are shuttling into and out of it and transferring their cargoes to other ships waiting outside the strait – adds to the cost and time and has created a global shortage, not of ships, but of tanker capacity because of the extra vessels tied up in the Middle East trade.The other dimension to the spike in prices is Donald Trump.

Advertisement

Trump stopped attacking Iran in late July in the hope that would take some of the heat out of the oil prices – and US gasoline and diesel prices – in the lead up to the US midterm elections.He has subsequently done everything he can – convincing the G7 to release strategic reserves of diesel, allowing tax-exempt diesel in the US (normally reserved for off-road usages) to be used on public roads and controversially (and probably illegally) lifting sanctions on Russia and striking a deal with Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel to the US.While none of those attempts to lower US domestic gasoline and diesel prices have had any material effect – gasoline prices are still 40 per cent higher than a year ago, diesel prices about 74 per cent higher and Trump’s poll numbers have plumbed new lows – Trump has maintained the moratorium on attacks.With the elections just over a week away, Trump’s rhetoric has hardened. On Thursday, he told reporters that “something one way or the other” would happen “fairly soon” with Iran. Then on Sunday, he said it was “getting to be decision time” on whether to strike a deal with Iran or re-start the attacks.

Advertisement

“I have a decision to make. Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal?” he said on Fox News.“That’s all. We don’t play games.”“Last time you wanted to ‘finish the job’ Iran emerged even stronger”: Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi is not backing down from Trump.APThe US has been moving diplomats and military staff out of the region and sending more military resources to the Middle East in preparation for an escalation of hostilities.The Iranians have vowed to retaliate if the US does resume its attacks.

Advertisement

“Last time you wanted to ‘finish the job’ Iran emerged even stronger,” its foreign affairs minister posted on social media.“Want to try your luck again? Be our guest. But be careful; we have unfinished jobs, too,” Abbas Araghchi wrote.‘I have a decision to make. Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal?’Donald Trump on Fox NewsIt’s that prospect of renewed conflict that seems to be the major influence over the surge in oil prices.There are, broadly, two markets that price oil. One is the futures market, which prices oil for delivery at some point in future, and the other, “Dated Brent,” is for physical delivery in the near term.

Advertisement

Dated Brent, which normally trades at a relatively modest premium – less than $US2 a barrel – to the futures price, was trading around $US125 a barrel late last week after a sudden jump late in the week, which might suggest a sudden urgency from buyers to get their hands on oil before a new round of violence erupts.The futures prices, in turn, might be surging in anticipation of the disruption that a renewed conflict will have to supply from the Middle East.Whatever the explanation, it would appear clear that traders believe there is both a significant probability that the war will flare up again and that flows through the strait and through the Saudi pipeline could be materially impacted despite Trump’s confidence that he can “finish it (the war) off” quickly.LoadingHe has, of course, expressed similar confidence since the US and Israel launched their attacks on February 28. Nearly eight months later, you’d have to say that confidence was misplaced.

Advertisement

The futures market pricing would suggest that traders, too, have little confidence that Trump and his “Department of War” can do in the near term what he has consistently failed to deliver over nearly eight months.The other dimension to the conflict and its impact on gasoline/petrol and diesel prices is that there has been significant damage to Middle Eastern oil refineries, while Ukraine’s very successful targeting of Russia’s refineries has also taken significant Russian supply out of the global market.Even if flows of oil from the Middle East could be sustained through renewed hostilities, flows of refined products will continue to be less than what they were before the two wars.No-one pumps crude oil into their cars or trucks, so the impact of the conflict where it hurts US and other consumers and companies will persist for some times beyond the end of the war, whenever – if ever – it ends.The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. news.title: Brazil election shock: anti-Israel Lula defeats Bolsonaro's son in stunning upset
news.text: Brazil's left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva scored a dramatic and unexpected victory overnight Sunday into Monday in the country's fiercely contested presidential election, defeating far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro. With 99.9% of the votes counted, Lula secured 51.77%, compared with 48.23% for Bolsonaro. Although relatively narrow, the margin was clear and decisive, defying polls that had predicted a razor-thin victory for Bolsonaro. Bolsonaro's defeat is a blow to U.S. President Donald Trump, who did not explicitly endorse him but would have seen his growing influence in Latin America expand further with a right-wing victory. Lula, by contrast, has frequently clashed with Trump. His victory is also unwelcome news for Israel. The incumbent president, who at 80 will begin his fourth nonconsecutive term, is one of Israel's fiercest critics worldwide and has repeatedly accused it of "genocide." Brazil uses electronic voting machines, allowing results to be counted rapidly overnight. Polling stations were originally scheduled to close Sunday at 5 p.m. local time (10 p.m. in Israel), but Lula's campaign petitioned to extend voting following reports of public transportation disruptions in several areas, including São Paulo. Brazil's Supreme Court subsequently extended voting nationwide by two hours. Bolsonaro's campaign also requested an extension, citing rainy weather in the country's south. Bolsonaro's defeat came as a surprise after he entered the decisive runoff as the favorite. In the first round earlier this month, when several other candidates were also competing, he finished first with 47% of the vote, compared with 45% for the incumbent. That result had surprised pollsters, who predicted Lula would finish first by a relatively comfortable margin. In the 2022 election, when Lula defeated his current rival's father, Jair Bolsonaro, his margin of victory was also much narrower than polls had forecast, prompting speculation that surveys were once again underestimating the younger Bolsonaro's support. Historical precedent had also favored Bolsonaro: Never before had a candidate who finished second in the first round of a Brazilian presidential election gone on to win the decisive runoff. That changed overnight with Lula's victory. The ideological divide between the two candidates could hardly have been greater. Bolsonaro, 45, and Lula, 80, hold sharply opposing views on a range of issues, from Brazil's relations with the United States to climate change and welfare policy. Lula's victory also dashed hopes among Latin America's right-wing movements that the conservative wave sweeping the region over the past year, with election victories in Chile, Peru and Colombia, would reach its most populous country and largest economy. Instead, Lula's reelection leaves Brazil and Mexico, Latin America's second-most populous country, led by President Claudia Sheinbaum, under center-left leadership. A victory visit to the Western Wall? As noted, incumbent President Lula secured his fourth nonconsecutive term overnight. He previously served as Brazil's president from 2003 to 2010 and won the presidency again in 2022. He was released from prison in 2019 after spending more than 500 days behind bars, and his corruption convictions were annulled in 2021. In recent months, he faced an increasingly difficult election campaign amid public dissatisfaction over the cost of living and concerns about personal security. His rival, Bolsonaro, made a tough stance on crime the cornerstone of his campaign and pledged to lower food prices. Bolsonaro, who has served as a senator since 2019, also promised judicial reform, which he planned to pursue in part through the next president's power to appoint at least three of the Supreme Court's 11 justices, with several retirements expected in the coming years. Bolsonaro and Lula also differ sharply in their attitudes toward Israel. Flávio Bolsonaro, like his father Jair, is a staunch supporter of Israel, and their political movement is known in Brazil for its support for Israel and the Jewish people. Israeli flags are traditionally displayed at rallies held by both father and son. At his final campaign rally Saturday in Barra da Tijuca, in Rio de Janeiro state, Flávio himself was filmed waving an Israeli flag. Earlier this year, the younger Bolsonaro made his fourth visit to Israel alongside his brother Eduardo. He toured Samaria in the northern West Bank, prayed at the Western Wall and pledged to move Brazil's embassy to Jerusalem. "We appreciate and love Israel," he said at the time. "We support Israel's right to defend itself in every way." Estevam Hernandes, Bolsonaro's personal pastor and one of his closest associates, who has accompanied him throughout the campaign, told ynet's Itamar Eichner in an interview Sunday that if Bolsonaro wins, he could make a victory visit to Israel as early as next month. "Flávio Bolsonaro is a man who loves Israel with all his heart. We agreed that we would celebrate his victory in Jerusalem. We will visit Israel in November and bring Brazil's future economy minister with us, and Flávio may join us as well. In any case, the plan is to bring Flávio to the Western Wall to celebrate the victory," Hernandes said. Lula, by contrast, has become one of Israel's fiercest critics worldwide during his current term, particularly since the October 7 massacre and the war in Gaza. In February 2024, he accused Israel of committing genocide, comparing its actions to those of Hitler. Two months later, he incorrectly claimed that more than 12 million children had been killed in the Gaza war. That same year, he recalled Brazil's ambassador from Israel, and in 2025 refused to approve the appointment of a new Israeli ambassador to Brasília. In his address to the UN General Assembly this past September, although he condemned Hamas, he also accused Netanyahu's government of "the genocide of women and children in Gaza." $12 million for a movie and a promise to pardon his father Both candidates have faced allegations of corruption involving family members and political allies. Bolsonaro himself is currently embroiled in a sprawling investigation into corruption, money laundering and tax evasion. As part of the affair, he acknowledged seeking approximately $12 million from Daniel Vorcaro, a former banker, to finance a film about his father's life. His father, Jair Bolsonaro, is still serving the 27-year prison sentence imposed after he was convicted of attempting a coup following his defeat to Lula in the 2022 election, although he is currently under house arrest for medical reasons. In the run-up to the vote, Lula repeatedly portrayed the younger Bolsonaro as a threat to democracy, while Bolsonaro pledged to pursue a pardon for his father if elected. Since his defeat in the first round, Lula has attempted to woo undecided voters with costly economic incentives. His government approved a debt-relief program for small businesses, among other measures, and promised free public transportation on weekends. But those efforts appeared to have fallen short. At a polling station in Rio de Janeiro, Elba Marques, a 75-year-old retiree, said her vote for Bolsonaro was a vote against Lula's Workers' Party rather than an endorsement of Bolsonaro himself. "I can't stand hearing the same man say for 40 years that he's going to fix Brazil. It's the same promise over and over again," she said. Bolsonaro, speaking after casting his ballot at a polling station in Rio de Janeiro earlier Sunday, said the time had come for change. "Brazil can’t take another four years the way things are ... Everyone’s life has got worse," he warned, as supporters nearby chanted, "Lula, thief, you belong in jail!" Lula: It's either our flag or the US flag Lula, meanwhile, once again sought to frame the election as a referendum on Brazil's independence, portraying his opponent as a proxy for U.S. President Donald Trump. Speaking to reporters after casting his ballot in his political stronghold of São Bernardo do Campo, near São Paulo, he accused Bolsonaro of wanting to "govern under the U.S. flag." Lula said Brazilians had to choose between someone who would defend their national flag and someone who would defend the American flag. Perhaps to reinforce that message, Lula also posed for photographs holding up the Brazilian flag inside the polling station. The remarks came against the backdrop of Lula's sharp criticism of Trump throughout the campaign and his warnings about attempted U.S. interference in Brazil's election. The Trump administration imposed steep tariffs on Brazilian exports, announced sanctions against the Supreme Court justice who oversaw the investigation that led to Jair Bolsonaro's conviction, and designated drug trafficking organizations as foreign terrorist organizations. Some experts suggested the latter move may have been intended to portray Lula as soft on crime. Flávio Bolsonaro, for his part, has boasted of his close ties to White House officials and insisted that Brazil must negotiate better deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare-earth minerals sector. Brazil's reserves are estimated at up to 21 million metric tons, second only to China's. Politically, however, Bolsonaro denies receiving assistance from the U.S. administration.
news.summary: Brazil halts Latin America's rightward wave as Lula, 80, who accused Israel of 'genocide' and clashed with Trump, wins a fourth term in a historic comeback over Flávio Bolsonaro, who vowed to move the embassy to Jerusalem and pardon his jailed father

news.title: NFL fans put on brave face in Paris as Steelers beat Saints with chaos in the city
news.text: The Pittsburgh Steelers defeated the New Orleans Saints in the NFL’s first-ever game in France that went off surprisingly well despite the protests and civil unrest all week in Paris leading up to the matchup. The NFL was questioned throughout the week after seeing violence, looting, vandalization and more occurring in Paris over widespread anger regarding public living costs, deteriorating public services and more. Even President Donald Trump admitted he was "worried about it," talking about the Steelers-Saints matchup. But the league, despite beloved soccer team Paris Saint-Germaine postponing its Saturday match to Monday due to the unrest, didn’t blink. news.title: Trump makes bizarre 'beautiful a**' comment as Nicki Minaj floated as new press secretary
news.text: Pop star Nicki Minaj has been floated as Donald Trump’s new press secretary after the President went on a bizarre tangent to comment on her ‘beautiful a**’. The ‘Super Bass’ singer was pictured chatting to Steven Cheung , the White House director of communications, on Sunday, October 25. Mr Cheung posted a clip of the interaction on X with the caption: “Ladies and gentlemen, I think we may have found the new White House Press Secretary!” On the same day, Ms Minaj, appeared at a campaign rally alongside Trump to drum up support for Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections. Before the 43-year-old behind mega-hit ‘Anaconda’ took to the stage, Trump went on a tangent from his speech to comment on her appearance. He told the rally in Port Huron, Michigan: “By the way, look at one hell of a beautiful a** before… Nicki Minaj . That’s hard to miss.” After the crowd cheered, the President added: “Stand up. That’s hard to miss. I hope Nicki was not insulted but we love Nicki. She has been with us for a long time.” Minaj later went on stage to talk up the President’s economic record. Polls suggest the Republicans are heading for losses on November 3, with 61 percent of voters saying they disapprove of the President at the time. While 38 percent say they do, a majority of the electorate also said they would prefer a Democrat-controlled Congress over a Republican-held Capitol. If the Democrats did score a big win, they would be able to frustrate the President’s legislative agenda and block bills. Trump is in need of a new press secretary after Katie Zachaira was reportedly sacked from the role after only five days, the shortest term for any White House press secretary. Her only media briefing lasted for around 15 minutes.
news.summary: The Super Bass and Anaconda singer spoke in support of Trump at a Republican rally on Sunday when the President went on a bizarre tangent to comment on her body
