news.title: Trump critic Lula wins reelection in Brazil, securing fourth presidential term
news.text:
RIO DE JANEIRO — Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of US President Donald Trump, was reelected Sunday in a result that provides relief to critics of Trump and keeps some distance between Latin America’s biggest economy and Washington.

With 100% of the vote counted, Brazil’s electoral court announced that the soon to be 81-year-old Lula held an unassailable lead. The announcement capped an evening of chaos at polling places across Brazil, following a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours. That decision by a Supreme Court justice may trigger legal action by opponent Flávio Bolsonaro.

His triumph bucks a trend in Latin America where increasing numbers of right-of-center presidental candidates allied with Trump have been winning, further extending the United States’ influence in the region. Lula’s victory leaves Mexico and Brazil, Latin America’s two most populous nations, with left-of-center leaders. It also positions Latin America’s largest economy, with a GDP of $2.6 trillion per year, to remain independent of the US, despite the pressure of increased tariffs imposed by Trump.

The announcement kicked off a celebration of supporters in and out the Sao Paulo hotel where Lula watched the count with First Lady Rosângela da Silva, allies, and friends.

Lula’s victory, if confirmed by electoral authorities, will give him his non-consecutive fourth term as president. The next term begins on Jan. 5, 2027.

It is the first time since Brazil’s military dictatorship ended in 1985 that the second-highest vote getter in the first-round elections won the presidency. Bolsonaro had 47% of the vote in the first round to Lula’s 45%, a difference of 2.2 million votes.

Lula and Sen. Bolsonaro have yet to address their supporters.

Sunday’s victory will likely be the last of the veteran leader’s political career. Lula began his political career in the 1970s as a union leader. He then helped found the Workers’ Party, which he represented as a presidential candidate three times until he finally won it in 2002. He was reelected four years later and was succeeded by one of his cabinet ministers, Dilma Rousseff, in 2010. She was reelected in 2014.

Rousseff was impeached for accounting maneuvering in 2016 amid a sprawling corruption probe, which also ensnared Lula. He tried to run for president again in 2018 but was jailed in March after being convicted.

Lula was released from prison after 580 days and saw Brazil’s Supreme Court annul his sentence after police found messages that showed the judge who convicted him was biased. He quickly became one of former President Jair Bolsonaro’s biggest critics and narrowly beat him in 2022.

Lula admitted in 2024, two years into the job, that his administration had done little that far to earn the support of his voters.

Since he lost the first round, Lula reorganized his campaign, appealed to young voters, put millions of Brazilians on the streets to defend democratic values and his legacy, raised fears of another Bolsonaro administration and boosted several government initiatives.

Lula also defended Brazil’s sovereignty and insisted that a Bolsonaro presidency would allow the US to exert control over Brazil.

He joins Trump and Nicaragua’s President Daniel Ortega — all age 80 — as the oldest presidents in the Americas.
news.summary: The veteran leader secured his non-consecutive fourth term, with his next term scheduled to begin on Jan. 5, 2027.
news.author: Associated Press

news.title: Trump Names JD Vance, Marco Rubio as Potential 2028 Presidential Contenders
news.text: Michigan: US President Donald Trump offered an early glimpse into the Republican Party’s political future, naming JD Vance and Marco Rubio among the prominent figures who could run for the White House in 2028. Trump praised the GOP for having a “great bench” of potential candidates compared to the Democrats.In an interview with FOX 2's Roop Raj ahead of a rally in Michigan, Trump was asked directly about potential presidential contenders for 2028. He said it was too early to identify a clear front-runner but stressed that the Republican Party had no shortage of strong candidates.“I could tell you who I think, but it's a little bit early,” Trump said.“We have great names — you have JD Vance, Marco Rubio, and many others. We have a great bench; they (Democrats) have no bench,” he added.Earlier, while leaving for the Michigan rally, Trump also addressed geopolitical and energy challenges arising from the Russia-Ukraine war. He reiterated that Washington would not allow global energy security to be compromised by the ongoing conflict.“We're not going to be hostage with the oil industry over something that, frankly, should've never started,” Trump asserted, reiterating his view that the war was preventable.Meanwhile, the November 3 midterm elections are shaping up as a crucial contest for control of both chambers of Congress. The outcome is expected to have significant implications for Trump's legislative agenda and the balance of political power in Washington.The United States midterm elections are nationwide votes held every four years at the midpoint of a president's term. These elections serve as a major political temperature check, with all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and approximately one-third of the Senate seats up for grabs.The political contest comes amid broader challenges for the administration, including economic concerns and declining approval ratings. The Wall Street Journal reported in September that Trump's approval rating had fallen to 37 per cent in its polling, marking a low for a president heading into midterm elections in the publication's polling history dating back to 1990.

news.title: Federal appeals court hears arguments in Trump administration's voting lawsuit against California
news.text:
A rare Sunday federal appeals court hearing for the Justice Department's voting lawsuit against California closed without a ruling.

The department requested that the court issue one by Tuesday prior to the scheduled 1 p.m. PDT hearing before the district court. 

The arguments followed a surprise appeal by the Trump administration, which claims a district judge did not act quickly enough to address the administration's allegations of roughly 20,000 potential noncitizen voters on the state's voter rolls. 

A three-judge panel that includes two appointees of President Donald Trump and one appointee of former President Joe Biden heard arguments on DOJ's efforts to segregate ballots from the alleged noncitizens. 

California officials have countered that the list is unverified and includes the names of lawful voters, despite recent charges announced by DOJ of roughly 28 individuals from the list accused of voting and immigration-related crimes.

Earlier the DOJ sent letters last week to every county in California asking local elections officials to help identify potential voters who may be in the U.S. illegally, according to a letter described to ABC News. 

"Within 48 hours, we ask that you commit to working with DOJ and DHS to identify who on the accompanying list is a citizen and who is not," according to a letter sent by Justice Department officials to every county in California and described to ABC News. "The Department strongly urges you and your agency to work with the Department of Justice to ensure the integrity of California's federal elections before taking actions that risk significant federal scrutiny and legal exposure."

Earlier this month, the DOJ filed suit against California accusing the state of failing to review a list of alleged noncitizens that the Trump administration claimed were sent mail-in ballots for next month's midterm election. 

In court papers filed earlier this week, Los Angeles officials said a preliminary analysis of 200 of the names on the 20,000-person list, included a "high percentage" of individuals who say they were born in the U.S. and many more who have no voting history at all. 

Of those 200 individuals, officials said, nearly 40% "indicate that they were born in the United States, which is strong evidence of citizenship; and 71.2% of the records have no voting history," according to a filing.

The Justice Department's rushed efforts to have an appeals court quickly rule on its lawsuit faced considerable skepticism from the three-judge panel in Sunday's emergency hearing. 

Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, repeatedly questioned whether the appeals court had jurisdiction to step in at this stage in the litigation, and expressed considerable constitutional concerns over the lawsuit itself. 

"I don't see how we have jurisdiction," Bennett said to DOJ attorney Matthew Donnelly after pressing him over the timeline of the government's decision to seeking emergency appeal when a hearing before the district judge is already set for this Tuesday. 

Donnelly claimed that the DOJ's decision to seek relief from the appeals court came after disclosures by the state of the numbers of mail-in ballots already being processed in advance of the election -- which number in the hundreds of thousands. 

But Bennett's most significant concerns appeared to be the nature of the lawsuit and it appearing to directly contradict the Constitution's Elections Clause -- which mandates that states have jurisdictions over the manner their elections are run. 

"How can it preempt something that is expressly authorized by a provision of the Constitution?" Bennett asked. "How can the legislature making laws with regard to the manner of holding elections be preempted by a criminal statute passed by the Congress, especially when both the Congress and the California Legislature have made it illegal for non-citizens to vote?" 

Donnelly repeatedly pointed to DOJ's position that the way California is administering its elections -- and not acting on the hard drive of potential 20,000 likely non-citizens -- infringes on the federal government's ability to enforce the federal statute barring voting by illegal immigrants.

That explanation didn't appear to sit well with Bennett, however, who pointed out that the Constitution specifically tasks Congress with jurisdiction over how states administer their elections and not the Judiciary. 

"How can we, a federal court, do what is reserved to Congress, which Congress, in my view, hasn't done?" Bennett asked. 

"Your Honor, I would just simply -- unfortunately -- disagree with you that 18 USC 611 is not an election law that fits in the power of Congress," Donnelly replied. 

The judges also appeared to express concern about last-minute intervention to force California to segregate certain mail-in ballots given the state has provided a declaration saying if such an order was implemented it could have a "catastrophic" impact on tabulating the upcoming election. 

Circuit Judge Patrick Bumatay, a Trump appointee, repeatedly pressed California's attorney Samuel Siegel over why an injunction wouldn't be appropriate to ensure non-citizens votes are being actively cast in the ongoing election. 

"Without an injunction, you will never know, correct?" Bumatay asked. "Because if -- if the ballots are cast and separated, then they're going to be tabulated, and there's no way of knowing." 

"Your Honor, we would respectfully disagree with that because of the number of steps that people have to take to attest to their citizenship, to declare consistent with what is required by both federal and state law that they are citizens when they register to vote," Siegel responded. 

Even as Bumatay's questioning suggested he had more sympathy to granting the government some kind of relief, both Bennett and Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, a Biden appointee, appeared unified that the extraordinary relief being sought by DOJ was not appropriate at this juncture. 

"That's why I have a problem with the relief that's being sought here because I just don't see -- Congress and the California legislature have said non-citizens can't vote, and this lawsuit is about 'we don't like the way you're sorting citizens from non-citizens, and I just don't see 611 as telling California how to do the sorting," Bennett said. 

"That's absolutely right, Your Honor, and to reiterate my earlier point, if the federal government, if the Executive Branch wants that authority in the first instance, they need to go ask Congress for it, they haven't done that," Siegel said. "They ask this court to short circuit the democratic process and issue an order, not just on the eve of an election, but as an election is underway." 

In closing remarks, Bennett said the panel "will try to decide this case as quickly as possible."
news.summary: A federal appeals court had a rare Sunday hearing in the Justice Department's voting lawsuit against California.
news.author: Alexander Mallin And Luke Barr,San Francisco

news.title: Lula, Brazil’s iconic working class president, wins historic fourth term in dramatic comeback
news.text:
SAO PAULO: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won an unprecedented fourth term on Sunday, the country’s electoral court said, in a shock result that defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put ​the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America.

Lula, an icon of the global left and the most dominant force in Brazilian politics this century, defeated Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. The senator had finished first in the election’s first round and hoped to revive his father’s far-right movement.

At times, Lula’s reelection looked like a long shot, as voters soured on him and his Workers’ Party after years of corruption scandals and rising prices, while sweeping societal changes left the former metalworker and union leader looking out of touch with an increasingly app-based economy and its growing ranks of informal workers.

Lula’s victory marks another comeback in a career full of them. The 80-year-old was jailed from 2018 to 2019 on corruption charges that were later overturned, paving the way for him to beat ‌Jair Bolsonaro in the ‌2022 election.

“He is a statesman, a giant,” leftist federal lawmaker Erika Hilton, who was with ​Lula ‌in ⁠Sao Paulo ​during ⁠the vote count, told Reuters.

UNLIKELY PATH TO VICTORY

Pollsters said better-than-expected turnout had powered Lula to victory. Leonardo Barreto, the co-founder of consultancy Think Policy, said voters had chosen Lula’s familiar embrace over Bolsonaro’s novelty.

“People today are choosing between change, with some apprehension, and a known path, which guarantees certain rights,” he said.

During the campaign, Lula pointed to a track record of falling poverty and inequality, while unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation hit record lows during his third term.

He warned Bolsonaro would cut welfare spending, backslide on social advances and hand over Brazil’s sovereignty to US President Donald Trump, whose State Department led a campaign to get the Bolsonaros back to power.

Lula’s win deprives Trump of a major addition to what has been a growing bloc of friendly right-wing ⁠Latin American governments that have embraced Washington’s agenda on security and migration.

Celso Amorim, a former Lula foreign ‌minister, told Reuters the leftist “would be very important for establishing a point of balance in Latin ‌America. Lula is that balance.”

COMEBACK KING

Lula becomes the first candidate since Brazil’s return ​to democracy in the 1980s to be elected after finishing second ‌in the first round.

Lula, who was president between 2003 and 2011, campaigned on a potent mix of pragmatism and populism that has shaped ‌his career in national politics for half a century, rolling out a slew of reforms aimed at improving the lives of workers and poor Brazilians.

These gained steam with late-campaign pledges that ranged from free nationwide weekend public transport, which has to be formally submitted to Congress, to a 15 percent increase in his trademark welfare program that is already being implemented.

Lula also championed a constitutional amendment that became Brazil’s biggest labor reform in decades, which passed with wide support in Congress.

CHALLENGING ‌LEGISLATIVE REALITY

Still, Lula’s fourth term could be his most difficult yet, after Brazil elected its most conservative Congress since returning to democracy in the 1980s.

Combined, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) and allied parties could control ⁠over 280 seats in the lower ⁠house and up to 50 seats in the Senate, enough for comfortable majorities in both chambers.

“He is likely to be a lame duck from the start,” said Oliver Stuenkel, a professor of international relations at the Getulio Vargas Foundation in São Paulo.

The incoming legislature will likely deepen recent trends of presidents ceding power to Congress, Stuenkel said, predicting Lula will face waning influence over Supreme Court nominations, unwieldy party coalitions, and even the threat of impeachment.

Lula faces an economy that his government forecasts will grow a meager 2.3 percent next year, adding to fiscal concerns tied to high interest rates and public debt that has risen past 82 percent of GDP, the highest since the pandemic.

The president’s critics blame spending, though interest costs have driven most of the increase in debt.

Goldman Sachs said it expects Lula to make modest progress at most to contain spending in a fourth term, as he stays committed to a state-led growth model.

Surging household debt also concerns economists. Trying to address the issue, Lula rolled out a provisional ban on online betting and unveiled a new debt relief program during the campaign.

The incoming right-wing Congress ​will try to pass structural reforms that favor businesses, experts say, ​prompting spending cuts that could fuel social upheaval.

news.title: LATIKA M BOURKE: Political hostility on the rise thanks to Trump, MAGA, Hanson and social media outrage
news.text:
In less than two weeks’ time, the verdict of the American people on Donald Trump’s second term will be in. The sheer nastiness of the campaign — along with last week’s horror attack on Australian MP Helen Haines — should give us our own moment to pause and reflect on the direction of our new era of politics.

In the US, the Democrats are confident. “Republicans’ path to keeping control of the House has all but evaporated,” said the independent, non-partisan Cook Political Report. Meanwhile, polling website Race to the WH, which has correctly predicted the Senate race in the last three elections, calculates a 72 per cent chance the Democrats could take the Senate, too.

The chief issue is the same one that helped Mr Trump return to the White House — the cost of living. The totem of this problem is fuel prices, which have shot to Biden-era pandemic highs thanks to Trump’s war in Iran, started in spite of his pledge not to start “Forever Wars”.

October will set the record for the most expensive month of US petrol prices ever. This record was also set for the last two months.

Unsurprisingly, the Reuters/Ipsos poll shows Mr Trump’s approval rating has tanked to a new low of 31 per cent, and his disapproval rating is at 66 per cent, up from 41 per cent at the time of his inauguration.

If the midterm results are bad for the Republicans, Mr Trump will no doubt attempt to spin his way out of them. But for now the record shows him having it both ways. He says he is not on the ballot, but he has poured enormous energy into rallying the MAGA faithful to turn out to vote, staging rallies in swing states and for key candidates.

One of those has been Vivek Ramaswamy, who, in a sign of the Republicans’ desperation, has taken US politics, polarisation and personal attacks to a new low. The candidate for governor of the state of Ohio released an ad featuring the mother of his Democratic rival, calling her daughter, Amy Acton, a liar.

But this was hardly political gold dust. Amy Acton and her brother were removed from their mother’s custody, when she was 12 years old, and their stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was charged with raping her. The last time Amy Acton set eyes on her mother in person was in the courtroom when her stepfather was arrested and indicted in 1978. He fled the state, evading prosecution, and died in 2004.

Amy Acton called the platforming of her mother “despicable” and “exploitative”.

That does not even cover it.

It is worth zooming out to appreciate what Mr Ramaswamy did.

He tried to frame his political opponent as a liar by exploiting a family breakdown triggered by her allegations of paedophilia at the hands of her stepfather. These claims were taken seriously enough in the late 1970s to warrant the removal of her and her brother from their mother’s care and led to a grand jury indictment.

Pitting family breakdowns into the political arena is gross at the most basic level, but to know it involves allegations of paedophilia is unforgivable, and it should especially disgust the MAGA supporters who pressed for the release of the Epstein Files.

Not that Ramaswamy, or the Republicans who matter, are even sorry. What they did next was worse. Instead of admitting the gross error of judgment and basic humanity, Vivek Ramaswamy claimed ownership and said he would spend $US4 million to air it.

When this tawdry affair reached the White House, what did the President and Vice President do?

“Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar,” US Vice President JD Vance said.

President Trump also cheered Vivek Ramaswamy on and told him to “ride with it”.

“I don’t care. If it were my mother speaking badly about me, you’d be making it the number one story on the news,” he told reporters.

“This has nothing to do with a stepfather or anything else. This has to do with the fact that a woman got out, the mother of a person running for governor of one of the greatest states, where I set records and said that she’s a liar.”

It has everything to do with the stepfather and far more.

Chris Christie, former Republican Governor of New Jersey, told the US ABC Network’s This Week: “This goes to the rotten moral core that Donald Trump has created for my party. And you then take probably two of the most prominent Trump wannabes in our party, JD Vance and Vivek Ramaswamy, and what they’re showing America is, we want to be just as morally bankrupt as Trump.”

“This is the future of our party if we don’t get our act together: to have charmless people with no charisma and the lack of moral clarity and centre that Donald Trump has.”

“One of the long-term impacts from this year’s election will be for Republicans in general, and Vice President Vance in particular, defending an ad that attempted to seek political gain from the rape of an underage girl,” Doug Sosnik, who advised then President Bill Clinton, told The Nightly.

Endorsing an attack ad over child rape is surely the end state of Donald Trump’s vitriolic brand of politics, which began with casual but still eyebrow-raising insults like “Crooked Hillary” and corrosive conspiracy theory questioning of opponents, such as the citizenship of the first Black president, Barack Obama.

Mr Trump’s success has been to execute so many shocking tactics that the public has become numb and desensitised to the gradual but now clear erasure of any standards in public life and campaigning.

In the United States, where political violence, just like gun violence, has become an accepted part of their culture, assassination attempts are hardly irregular. High-profile attempts have been made on President Trump himself, former speaker Nancy Pelosi and the US Congresswoman Gabby Giffords. January 6 and the presidential pardoning of those convicted for their insurrection crimes has all but given a green light to anyone else contemplating violent methods.

But those outside America do not have to accept this as their destiny.

MAGA’s exploitation of child rape should serve as a midterm moment for all those involved in public life and setting standards, and especially for those abroad who think copying the Make America Great Again formula will make them electorally successful at home.

Well before Helen Haines’ attacker was identified in the media, and his social media posts, which show an assortment of far-left and pro-climate change leanings, were exposed, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson rushed to News 24 airwaves to concede an error.

This related to a cartoon she had published on social media mocking independent Senator Jacqui Lambie for a health condition. She said she now believed the cartoon was not appropriate, that she had not seen it herself and that it would be taken down. Originally, she had told Senator Lambie to “lighten up,” despite now claiming she had not seen it before it went out.

Weeks earlier, she was on the back foot over a cartoon that called the former SAS Captain and federal Liberal MP Andrew Hastie a traitor. Ms Hanson is not the only one reassessing. The Labor Cabinet Minister Clare O’Neill in February deleted a post in which she referenced being ready to “smash some Liberals” having just “smashed” a Pilates class. She removed the post that afternoon, after it, rightly, triggered an outcry.

Words do matter. On the weekend, Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett said as plainly as a public servant could that the AFP monitors a direct relationship between those cartoons and an uptick in threats made against politicians.

On X, Pauline Hanson shot back: “The Please Explain cartoons have nothing to do with the tragic attack on Helen Haines. They will not be going anywhere,” she said. Senator Hanson, who blocks the ABC and The Guardian from press events, accused her critics of wanting to censor her.

These same cartoons have depicted former Labor Victorian premier Dan Andrews being run over and independent Senator Lidia Thorpe under the wheels of a vehicle. If these are meant to be jokes, Senator Hanson can and should find better ways to make the public laugh. Her cartoons have been an innovation in political communication and an effective way of skewering government incompetence when others have been too timid; to ensure their continued success, she needs to enforce better quality control to ensure that they don’t become a liability.

This has zero to do with cancelling or censoring. And it certainly does not mean letting our political leaders off the hook when they are performing badly. It should be clear that if you need to depict harm to your opponent, mock their health or accuse them of treachery, whatever political argument you were trying to make was long lost. Being nasty is not clever, and we are about to find out if it is even electorally successful for President Trump and his acolytes.

You don’t need an intelligence officer to tell you that in our hyper-connected world, the path to online radicalisation is now so swift and silent that it can be easy to miss. It can happen in days. The metric of political content is not whether the target of the attack should have big enough shoulders, but whether the content could inspire or even incite someone who is disaffected, mentally disturbed or prone to radical ideologies.

Australians have always been able to biff with vigour and do it well. The nation hardly has a reputation for being shrinking violets. So as Americans prepare to have their say on President Trump’s methods, so too can we.
news.summary: LATIKA M BOURKE: Political nastiness is reshaping the way democracies function and campaign.
news.author: Latika M Bourke

news.title: Putin Goon Issues Bloodthirsty Plea to Trump
news.text:
Vladimir Putin’s second-in-command has begged President Donald Trump to put a hit on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Dmitry Medvedev, the former Russian president and prime minister who remains one of Putin’s closest allies, delivered a vicious online tirade telling Trump to order the assassination of Zelensky, whom he called a “festering green parasite.”

“What should Trump do with such a ‘son of a b---h?’ American history itself offers a solution,” he wrote on the Kremlin-backed social media site Max, according to the Daily Mail and RBC-Ukraine. “All he has to do is summon the secretary of war and the CIA director and tell them to take care of this ‘unfortunate little problem.’”

He continued, “After all, the man does far more damage to Trump’s real interests than all the fallout from Trump’s imaginary grievances against Venezuela, Cuba, and Iran combined. The how, where, and by what means are irrelevant.”

Medvedev, who currently serves as deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, asked why Trump should “have any reason to like the twitchy little bloodsucker.”

He said that Zelensky “pestered Trump like a fat green fly, rudely demanding money and weapons to keep the war against Russia going” and “manipulated” Western leaders “working day in and day out to turn them against Trump and his team.”

Furthermore, he said the Ukrainian leader “repeatedly told Trump and his aides to get lost whenever they floated proposals for negotiating an end to the conflict” and that “through his reckless behavior, brought the United States and NATO to the brink of a global nuclear confrontation with Russia.”

“In short, the Kiev scumbag regularly spits straight in the face of the US president, ignoring his demands and turning influential Americans [and not-so-influential Europeans] against him,” Medvedev said. “To this festering green parasite, the president of the United States is a nobody. Which doesn’t stop him and his entire Nazi gang from repeatedly fleecing the Americans for enormous sums of money.”

“So much for ‘he may be a son of a b---h, but he’s our son of a b---h,’” he concluded.

The Daily Beast has reached out to the White House for comment.

The Kremlin goon’s diatribe came not long after Trump’s own special envoy, Steve Witkoff, praised Putin during a meeting in St. Petersburg last week, calling the brutal dictator a “humanitarian.”

“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” he told Putin. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that. I commend you, and I thank you again.”

It also comes amid the 80-year-old president’s frequent and aggressive criticisms of Zelensky, whom he blames for the war that Putin started in 2022.

Trump has called for Zelensky to be replaced as peace negotiator and even as Ukraine’s president, while simultaneously lauding Russia and saying the superpower has “been fine on Ukraine” and “haven’t been doing much” when it comes to wartime aggression.

news.title: Brazil’s Lula wins re-election, defeating Trump ally Bolsonaro
news.text: Brazil’s president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was re-elected after defeating conservative challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in Sunday’s presidential runoff, the country’s electoral authority announced, keeping Latin America’s largest economy under left-wing leadership.With more than 78% of votes counted, Lula was leading with 51.21% against Bolsonaro’s 48.79%, according to Reuters’ live election coverage. Pollster Datafolha projected Lula to win before the electoral authority confirmed his victory.The result is a setback for US President Donald Trump’s allies in Latin America. A Bolsonaro victory would have marked a rightward shift in Brazil, the region’s most populous country and largest economy, while Lula’s win leaves Brazil and Mexico with left-of-centre leaders.Flávio Bolsonaro, a senator and son of imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro, had campaigned on closer ties with Washington and promised to secure better deals with the Trump administration. Lula had criticised US policies towards Brazil, including tariffs on Brazilian exports and the designation of drug-trafficking groups as foreign terrorist organisations.The contest pitted two sharply polarised political camps against each other, with differences spanning relations with the United States, crime, climate policy and social welfare. Lula, who previously governed Brazil from 2003 to 2010, had sought an unprecedented fourth term.Lula supporters celebrate victoryLula supporters celebrated as the results showed him pulling ahead. Reuters reported World Cup-like scenes in Rio de Janeiro’s Laranjeiras neighbourhood, where people gathered in bars to follow the count and began singing as Lula overtook Bolsonaro.In downtown São Paulo, supporters at a nightclub cheered the news of Lula’s projected win.“I’ve been optimistic about Lula winning since the first round, even with Flávio in the lead,” Lucas dos Santos, a 29-year-old biomedical scientist, told Reuters.Julia Bueno, a 28-year-old technology worker, said she had attended a rally for Lula on Saturday and wanted to be near Avenida Paulista so she could join celebrations as soon as his victory was announced.“I was at the Saturday rally, and it was so moving. Both candidates had sought extensions in some areas, but for different reasons: Lula cited problems with buses transporting voters in nine states, while Bolsonaro pointed to heavy rain in the south.The order raised logistical concerns because some polling stations had already closed. In Brasilia, volunteers overseeing the count debated whether they needed to remain after the announcement. At a polling station in Rio de Janeiro, voting machines had been switched off and could not be restarted, according to the Associated Press.Bolsonaro had led Lula by more than 2.2 million votes in the first round earlier this month. More than 33 million of Brazil’s nearly 160 million voters had not turned out.The runoff was a rematch between two political forces that have divided the country. Lula defeated Jair Bolsonaro by the narrowest margin since Brazil’s return to democracy in 1985 in the previous presidential election four years ago.Cost of living and security shape campaignLula faced a difficult re-election battle amid voter concerns over rising living costs and crime. Bolsonaro made a tough-on-crime platform central to his campaign and promised to lower food prices, while Lula offered costly incentives in an effort to win over undecided voters.Both camps have faced corruption allegations involving allies and family members. Bolsonaro has been implicated in a sprawling scandal, while Lula spent more than a year in prison after corruption convictions that were later annulled.As Bolsonaro voted at a school in Rio de Janeiro, supporters shouted, “Lula, thief, your place is in prison,” while Lula’s supporters chanted in his favour.“The time of real change has arrived,” Bolsonaro said before the result. “Brazil can’t go on for another four years on its current trajectory.”Lula’s supporters said they backed him because of his record of supporting marginalised communities and reducing poverty.“Lula is a man of the people and he knows what it’s like to be poor,” Luzia da Souza, who runs a bar in Rio de Janeiro, told AP. “I find it impossible not to vote for him.”Anderson Falcão, a 43-year-old journalist in Brasilia, said he was concerned about Bolsonaro’s long-term political vision, which he described as “exclusionary”.“It’s a project that harms the less fortunate, harms the worker, women, the forest, the Amazon,” he said.Bolsonaro supporters, many wearing Brazil’s yellow and green jerseys, said they wanted change. Fabianne Borges Santoro, a 45-year-old physiotherapist in Rio de Janeiro, said prices were high and taxes too steep. She added that she had previously voted for Lula’s party but now associated it with corruption.Trump administration looms over electionThe Trump administration’s approach to Brazil became a central issue in the campaign. Lula criticised Trump over tariffs imposed on Brazilian exports and the US designation of drug-trafficking groups as foreign terrorist organisations. Experts said the measures may have been intended to portray Lula as weak on crime.Flávio Bolsonaro highlighted his ties to the White House and argued that Brazil needed better deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare-earth minerals sector. Brazil estimates that it holds deposits of up to 21 million tonnes, second only to China. Bolsonaro denied receiving assistance from the US government.Trump said on Sunday that he was following the election but declined to endorse either candidate.You use AI every day. news.title: President Lula has been re-elected, Brazil's electoral authority has declared
news.text:
President Lula has been re-elected, Brazil's electoral authority has declared

On Sunday, Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva was re-elected in a blow to US President Donald Trump.

The result over rival Flávio Bolsonaro, is the first time any president of Brazil has overturned a loss in the first round of voting, since democracy returned to the nation in 1988.

Lula, 81, secured 51.76% of the vote against Bolsonaro’s 48.24% after 99.81% of the votes were counted.

Polls were on a knife-edge throughout the stages of counting, with Bolsonaro slightly ahead for much of this time, according to the BBC.

The result followed scenes of chaos in polling stations throughout Brazil after the Supreme Court justice ruled at the last minute to extend voting by two hours, delaying the result by just over two hours.

This decision could trigger legal action to overturn the result by Bolsonaro. 

Bolsonaro beat Lula in the first round of voting on October 4th, and many voters and political commentators doubted Lula would be able to reverse his fortunes in just three weeks.

With other major Latin American countries already under Trump-allied conservative governments - including Argentina, Chile and Colombia - Brazil has bucked the previous trend for voters in the region kicking out left-wing candidates in favour of populist alternatives.

Alongside Mexico, the result means Brazil remains a left-of-centre government sceptical of Trump’s policies in the region.

With a GDP of $2.6 trillion per year, Brazil is Latin America’s largest economy. That it will now remain largely independent of Trump’s policy in the region, will be regarded as a blow to his ambitions in Latin America.

The news was greeted with celebrations by Lula’s supporters in and around the Sao Paulo hotel where he watched the count alongside his wife, First Lady Rosangela da Silva.

This is a breaking news story - more information to follow
news.summary: He beat right of center rival Flávio Bolsonaro to win a fourth term in office

news.title: Todd Blanche challenges Dana Bash for only citing part of Constitution during heated election clash
news.text: Attorney General Todd Blanche confronted CNN host Dana Bash on Sunday after the network highlighted only the first portion of the Constitution's Elections Clause during a heated exchange on "State of the Union" over the Justice Department's lawsuit concerning two candidates with similar names in Alaska's closely watched Senate race. Blanche pushed back as Bash referenced the Alaska Supreme Court's earlier ruling allowing Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., who shares a name with incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, to remain on the ballot. The attorney general demanded that CNN display the remainder of the constitutional provision, which grants Congress authority to make or alter regulations governing congressional elections. "Conveniently, you put up the Constitution on your screen, but you highlighted only the first clause. Why don't you show the next clause to your viewers, which says that Congress is allowed to pass laws to make sure that that happens? Put that back up there," Blanche said. BLANCHE WON'T RULE OUT DOJ BLOCKING ELECTION CERTIFICATION IN 'DOOMSDAY' SCENARIO The exchange centered on Article I, Section 4 of the Constitution, which gives state legislatures authority to establish procedures for congressional elections while permitting Congress to enact or modify those regulations. Blanche argued that the second half of the provision supports the federal government's intervention under existing federal statutes. "The second clause says that the Congress may at any time by law, and we have a law, and that's the law that we're relying on when we filed suit earlier this week," Blanche said. The Justice Department’s lawsuit relies on the National Voter Registration Act, arguing that allowing a candidate who, according to the DOJ, intends to confuse voters to remain on the ballot undermines election integrity. The complaint asks the court to delay election certification if votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. could alter the final outcome. The DOJ's complaint accused the challenger of deliberately attempting to mislead voters by using a name similar to the incumbent's. DOJ OFFICIAL DEFENDS TRUMP'S NONCITIZEN VOTER PROBE ON '60 MINUTES,' ACCUSES SHOW OF EDITING OUT HER ANSWERS Media Research Center President David Bozell criticized Bash's presentation of the constitutional language in a statement to Fox News Digital, accusing CNN of failing to provide viewers with the complete provision. "An anchor who hands viewers half a provision on election integrity is running a magic act, and the trick fell apart on live television. Bash's job is to give the audience the full text up front. CNN owes its dozens of viewers the whole clause, and a better editor," Bozell said. The DOJ lawsuit follows a June ruling by the Alaska Supreme Court allowing the challenger to appear on the ballot despite objections from state election officials. The court left the question of how his name should appear to the state's Division of Elections. "Daniel J. Sullivan decided to run for Senator in 2026 as a Republican with the intention of misleading supporters of Senator Sullivan into voting for him," the complaint states. BLANCHE ANNOUNCES CHARGES AGAINST 10 PERMANENT RESIDENTS ACCUSED OF MINNESOTA VOTER FRAUD Republicans have accused the challenger, a retired teacher from Petersburg, of attempting to siphon votes from the incumbent. Daniel J. Sullivan has denied those accusations and maintained that his candidacy is legitimate. President Donald Trump also addressed the controversy Friday while speaking to reporters in Florida, acknowledging that he personally encouraged the Justice Department to pursue legal action. "I'm the one that said, do it," Trump said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The federal challenge faces opposition from voting rights groups and the campaign of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, both of which filed motions to intervene in the case. The American Civil Liberties Union argued that the National Voter Registration Act establishes voter-registration procedures and does not authorize blocking election certification over candidate placement.
news.summary: Todd Blanche demanded CNN show the full Elections Clause in the Constitution on air after Dana Bash highlighted only the first portion during a tense legal debate.

news.title: Lula wins fourth term in Brazil but faces hostile Congress and divided country
news.text:
Brazil's veteran left-wing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has been re-elected after a bitter campaign, defeating his right-wing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro.

It is Lula's fourth win in a presidential election, having served two terms as president from January 2003 to December 2010, and again from January 2023.

But the road to his win in Sunday's run-off was not smooth.

Bolsonaro beat Lula in the first round on 4 October, and many did not think he could turn the result around in just three weeks.

He has also bucked a wider Latin American trend, where voters have punished incumbents and turned right. Across the region, larger countries such as Argentina, Chile and Colombia all now have conservative leaders at their helm.

Lula's campaign sprang back to life following his first-round defeat, driven by street demonstrations and a massive social media push.

The former metalworker, who has dominated Brazil's left since he first ran for president in 1989, nevertheless faces the most challenging political landscape since he first took office in 2003.

His new term, set to begin on 5 January 2027, will start amid significant constraints at home and abroad, including animosity from US President Donald Trump.

While Trump did not endorse Lula's rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, directly, as he did with the right-wing candidates who went on to win presidential elections in Colombia and Honduras, there is little doubt his administration would have preferred a conservative at the helm of this country of 213 million people.

The White House regards Latin America as an area of US influence, and the Trump administration is keen to have leaders in power who support its policies, including on defence, security, and trade.

It is also keen to reduce China's influence in the Western Hemisphere.

Brazil, oil-rich and home to the world's second-largest reserves of rare earth minerals, is the only major country in South America not governed by a right-wing leader, with Lula widely seen as China-friendly.

Flávio Bolsonaro had promised to align Brazil more closely with Washington, while Lula warned the US not to interfere in the election and insisted Brazil would "never fit into anyone's backyard".

But while the White House may be disappointed, environmentalists will welcome Lula's victory, having feared that a Bolsonaro win would have given Brazil's influential agribusiness and mining sectors more power.

They pointed to record levels of deforestation and forest fires in the Amazon during his father Jair's presidency, arguing that under the younger Bolsonaro's laxer environmental policies, destruction could recur in this key ecosystem.

While Lula's supporters are ecstatic about his victory, the result shows that the country remains deeply divided, with more than 48% of voters choosing Bolsonaro.

In addition to the challenge of uniting such a deeply polarised country, Lula will have to govern alongside the most right-wing Congress in Brazil's democratic era.

Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL) was the party that made the biggest gains in the election.

Yet Lula's Workers' Party organised huge rallies ahead of the run-off, showing the strong grassroots support it commands.

Before the election, Lula had described the poll as "a parting of the waters for Brazil".

He promised to bridge the gap between Brazil's opposing political poles with "a new way of governing", adding in a WhatsApp livestream before the election that "this country will never be the same again".

While he offered little detail on what the new way of governing would entail, he insisted he would "remain firm in the fight for a more just country, with opportunities for all and policies directed at the needs of the population".

With a largely hostile Congress, this fight just may prove much harder for the veteran leader - who will be 85 by the end of his fourth term - than in his three previous terms in office.
news.summary: Brazil's veteran left-wing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has been re-elected after a bitter campaign, defeating his right-wing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro.

How is the Israeli election shaping up and just what might it mean for Palestine? 

Netanyahu’s main competitor is different to him in a lot of ways, but on Gaza they share similar positions.

12.06am, 26 Oct 2026

Share options

ON TUESDAY, VOTERS in Israel will go to the polls in what is being dubbed one of the most consequential elections since the State’s foundation in 1948. 

Benjamin Netanyahu, the country’s longest-serving prime minister, is seeking to retain power, but he faces a tight race. 

Former IDF chief, Gadi Eisenkot, is Netanyahu’s top rival in the election, with polls placing the two neck and neck ahead of the 27 October vote.

His Yashar party is a new one, formed in 2025, a year after Eisenkot resigned from Netanyahu’s war cabinet after 11 months. 

He joined the cabinet in the wake of Hamas’ October 7 attack in 2023, in which nearly 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken back to Gaza as hostages, but tendered his resignation over his concern that Netanyahu had no plan for after the war on Hamas.

Eisenkot (66) says he is running to “save Israel”. He argues Netanyahu is pushing the country towards authoritarianism and has dragged Israel into “forever wars”, damaging its standing internationally. 

Gadi EisenkotAlamy

Much has been written about how the two men are opposites of each other in a lot of ways:

Where Netanyahu is bombastic with a fluent command of the English language, Eisenkot has limited English and is seen as serious and uncharismatic – something Netanyahu has sought to use against him, arguing that this, coupled with his lack of political experience, would allow world leaders to push him around.

Eisenkot’s working-class roots also come in contrast to Netanyahu, who comes from an elite family and whose father was a prominent professor in the United States.

The death of Eisenkot’s son, Gal, who was killed fighting in Gaza in December 2023, has contributed to Eisenkot’s popularity, with many voters in Israel empathising with his loss and grief.

But just how different are his policies from Netanyahu’s? 

Israel’s security and accountability for October 7 have been two focal points of this election. 

Eisenkot has pledged to launch a national inquiry into how the Hamas attack was handled, something Netanyahu’s government, which was in power at the time, has rejected. 

Eisenkot has sought to appeal to centrist and liberal voters by pledging to “protect judicial independence, the rule of law, minority rights and a free press”.

He has also promised to try to restore the international image of Israel, badly strained after three years of war and genocide in Gaza and violence in the occupied West Bank.

He has vowed to crack down on West Bank settlers who have attacked Palestinians with impunity and recently beat up an American journalist and a French mayor, decrying the incidents as “Jewish terror” abetted by Netanyahu’s government.

But the military man is no peacenik. He has even sought to play to the right of Netanyahu by vowing no Palestinian State, replaying clips from an earlier political era in which the long-serving prime minister begrudgingly voiced openness to the idea under US pressure.

Commanding the military during the 2006 war with Hezbollah, Eisenkot devised the so-called “Dahiya doctrine”, named after a Beirut suburb, in which Israel vowed massive force against civilian infrastructure in areas populated by the Lebanese militants.

Advertisement

Israel has adopted the doctrine again in Gaza, causing destruction that critics say amounts to war crimes, an assertion disputed by Israel.

On Gaza, Eisenkot has vowed to end Hamas rule within 18 months.

He said this could be achieved either through the implementation of US President Donald Trump’s ceasefire plan, which envisages Hamas’s gradual disarmament and a transfer of power, or through “creative operations” aimed at destroying the movement’s military wing.

All in all, when it comes to Palestine, an electoral win for Eisenkot would not result in any sweeping policy changes. 

Outcome and fringe actors

Tuesday’s vote is expected to be close, with more than half a million young Israelis due to vote for the first time.

Surveys show they overwhelmingly identify as centre-right or right-wing.

A poll of 543 first-time voters published by Israeli outlet Ynet showed some 16 per cent supporting either far-right Ben Gvir’s ultranationalist Otzma Yehudit party or the far-right Religious Zionism party of finance minister Bezalel Smotrich.

Polls show Gvir’s party winning eight or nine seats in the 120-member parliament (known as the Knesset), making it the first time it will win a mandate running as a standalone entity.

Gvir, who has been convicted at least eight times in Israeli courts before becoming minister, on charges including supporting a terror organisation and incitement to racism, has become the firebrand face of Israel’s far-right.

His political influence has skyrocketed since joining Netanyahu’s coalition four years ago.

As national security minister with responsibility for the police, Gvir has helped more than 200,000 Israelis gain access to firearms and boasts frequently about the worsening conditions for Palestinian detainees in Israeli jails.

Ben GvirAlamy

And he has used his place in the cabinet to push the government to take more maximalist positions in Israel’s multi-front wars.

The lawyer-turned-politician was barred from serving in the military in his youth over his support for extremist right-wing groups.

Now, he says he will demand the defence minister post if Netanyahu’s bloc wins again on 27 October.

Israel uses a proportional representation voting system, which has meant governments have always been coalitions of multiple parties.

As a result, it may take weeks or even months before the next government is formed.

In the three-year period between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five separate elections as parties could not form a coalition. 

The official result for this year’s election is set to be published on 4 November, with preliminary results published next Wednesday.

news.title: Trump Shares News of B.C. Conservatives’ Election Win
news.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump shared news of the B.C. Conservatives’ majority government win in an Oct. 25 post on Truth Social.

Trump shared a link to a report by media outlet Just the News, reposting its headline: “Conservative Party wins in British Columbia for first time in almost 100 years.” The president made no other comment in the post.

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra shared Trump’s post on X the same day.

The B.C. Conservatives won 64 seats in the province’s Oct. 24 snap election, securing a majority with 48.05 percent of the vote. The NDP won 27 seats with 37.37 percent of the vote, while the Green Party retained two seats in the provincial legislature.

The B.C. NDP previously won 47 seats after winning a slim majority in the October 2024 election, with the Conservatives winning 44 sates and the Green Party wining 2.

The B.C. Conservatives’ victory marks the party’s first majority government in the province since 1928, when Simon Fraser Tolmie led the party to victory.

Incumbent Premier and NDP Leader David Eby called the snap election on Sept. 22, initially framing it as a response to an “existential moment” due to the tariffs imposed by Trump.

At a press conference later that day, Eby told reporters he was seeking a clear mandate from British Columbians to choose between an NDP government and a Conservative one, which he said would acquiesce to U.S. demands.

Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson has also criticized Trump’s tariffs on Canada, promising in a Sept. 25 statement to take action to stand up to the U.S. president.

When you boil down the essence of the alleged Russian military threat to America’s homeland security it amounts to just plain barking idiocy; it’s so out to lunch as to be offensive to even a modicum of human intelligence.

As we have seen in Parts 1 & 2, any conceivable threat of a Russian nuclear attack on the American homeland is already in deep checkmate.

That’s because America’s bought and paid for strategic nuclear triad, which bears a de minimis annual operating, maintenance and replacement cost of just $75 billion per year, has upwards of 900 warheads lined up to survive a first strike; and to then deliver a civilization-ending retaliatory strike to the Russian homeland that would be the equivalent of 13,000 Hiroshima’s. It would kill and injure 90 million Russians or 65% of its entire population of men, women and children within hours.

Accordingly, no Russian leader – whether as rational as Putin or a military putsch down the road – would ever give an unprovoked nuclear first strike attack on America a second thought. It’s not remotely in the cards of any future history, and therefore provides zero reason for Washington’s meddling in Ukraine on Russia’s doorstep.

Moreover, the alternative theoretical threat of a conventional military assault on the home territory of America is even more ludicrous. Russia does not remotely have the naval firepower and air-and sea-lift capacities to get even a 500 soldiers to the New Jersey shores, let alone the million-man lethally armed, supported and continuously re-supplied combatant units that would be needed for an invasion of the US that could make a difference.

Again, they have not a single serviceable aircraft carrier, no fully equipped carrier battle groups and a decrepit surface Navy of aging cruisers, destroyers, and frigates, many of Soviet-era design and dispersed across separated fleets. Altogether this remnant of the Soviet era Navy amounts to 1.4 million displacement tons or just of the 8.0 million tons of state-of-the-art surface and attack submarine combatants fielded by the US Navy.

For want of doubt, just consider what would happen to a Russian invasionary armada owing to the 50 cruise-missile equipped US attack submarines that would be lying in wait at the choke points far from the US shores. To wit, this isn’t November 1941 one when six Japanese aircraft carriers – Akagi, Kaga, Sōryū, Hiryū, Shōkaku, and Zuikaku – mbarked silently and unseen on the blue waters of the Western Pacific on the way to Pearl Harbor.

To the contrary, the only place in the world were Russia could assemble a expeditionary fleet of the requisite scale to attack America would be in Sevastopol on the Crimean peninsula. The latter has been its primary warm water port since it was purchased by Catherine the Great from the Ottoman’s in 1783, not stolen from Ukraine in 2014 as the Washington narrative falsely claims.

Here’s the thing. The US Navy usually has two to three carrier battle groups in the vicinity of the Mediterranean Sea and could mobilize more if needed to block the route from Sevastopol to Gibraltar shown below. And, even more lethally, it also has a double digit numbers of the current Los Angeles class, Seawolf-class and state of the art Virginia Class attack submarines that could conduct a shooting gallery exercise at all the choke points along the way. That is, at the Bosporus Strait in Turkey, the narrow passage around the boot of Italy and Sicily, and most especially at the mere 8-mile wide channel at the Pillar of Heracles (Gibraltar).

The truth is, no Russian military leaders would ever send their surface navy on this kind of suicide voyage from Sevastopol to Gibraltar. Unlike in 1941, Washington’s eye’s in the sky would know the minute that Russia began to assemble even a few boats for an armada to be launched from Sevastopol; and a president from either party, like JFK in the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, would tell the Kremlin forthwith that the only purpose of such an naval armada would not be to rescue Russian fisherman stranded in Rio de Janeiro, but to attack the homeland of America.

Accordingly, Russia would be told that its Black Sea fleet would be sunk the minute it passed through the Bosporus or beyond, and that would be the end of the Russian invasion of America then and there. The Kremlin would either turn back the fleet in the Black Sea or find it incommunicado in the Davy Jones’ Locker, Mediterranean division.

Moreover, that ain’t the half of it. Even if it managed to get a partial badly battered fleet through Gibraltar, it would be barely halfway through its journey from Sevastopol to the shores of Florida, New Jersey, the Chesapeake Bay or New York Harbor. So whatever would be left of the armada would find a watery grave along the huge expanse of the Atlantic Ocean’s vasty deep during the second half of the route.

Stated differently, unlike the Spanish Armada in 1588, the putative Russian Armada would never get even a glimpse of the American coast line – other than on their iPhones on the way down to the bottom of the seas.

So that’s the sum and substance of the Russian military threat to the USA homeland: To wit, their ain’t none.

Again, therefore, the question recurs. Why are we in Ukraine or why even do we still maintain 100,000 military personnel in Europe in bases scattered all around the continent?

The answer is, of course, is not to protect our European NATO allies from an invasion by the Rooskies. For crying out loud, whatever Putin’s faults may be, he isn’t stupid.

Just look at the societal basket cases in Europe today – exemplified by the chaos on the streets of France and Italy, the self-imposed unraveling of the German industrial economy and the woke la la land called England. Why in the hell would Putin ever want to invade these socialist economic disasters – even if he had the military and fiscal wherewithal, which he most definitely does not.

And least we forget, the Russians actually know from bitter experience where socialism actually leads. So here’s where France is going – to fiscal hell in a hand basket. That is to say, France doesn’t need the US military to rescue it from Putin – the latter has long ago said no thanks. And and with respect to all of Europe in its waning days, too.

So the whole bloody $150 billion mess of the US regime change intervention in Ukraine since the CIA-led coup in February 2014 boils down to another hoary narrative from the War Capital of the World: Namely, the giant lie that Ukraine was a long-standing independent country minding its own business, and was then invaded by a land-hungry Putin on a totally unprovoked basis.

For want of doubt, here is a summary of why the very opposite is true. To wit, there never was a legitimate country throughout all of post-medieval history called “Ukraine”. The latter was an utterly capricious and subsequently blood soaked set of unnatural borders of an administrative unit within the Soviet Empire. As shown below, all the parts and pieces within the current allegedly sacrosanct borders of “Ukraine” were actually seconded from Czarist Russia or stolen from neighboring countries by Lenin, Stalin and Khrushchev.

Accordingly, there is no case whatsoever that Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 was “unprovoked” and unrelated to NATO’s own transparent provocations in the region. The very idea that this entire misbegotten Washington enterprise since February 2014 has been undertaken in the defense of the “rule of law” and the sanctity of borders is just plain insidious propaganda.

The details are arrayed below, but the larger issue needs be addressed first.

Namely, is there any reason to believe that Russia is an aggressive, expansionist power looking to gobble up neighboring countries which were not integral parts of its own historic evolution, as is the case with Ukraine per the amplification below?

After all, if Trump does manage to strike a Ukraine peace and partition deal in the near future, would that in any way, shape or form amount to the modern day Munich appeasement analogy that the neocons so loudly proclaim?

The answer to these questions, however, is a resounding no!

Our firm rebuke of the hoary Munich analogy as it has been falsely applied to Putin is based on what might be called the double-digit rule. To wit, the true expansionary hegemons of modern history have spent huge parts of their GDP on defense because that’s what it takes to support the military infrastructure and logistics required for invasion and occupation of foreign lands.

For instance, here are the figures for military spending by Nazi Germany from 1935–1944 expressed as a percent of GDP. This is what an aggressive hegemon looks like in the ramp-up to war: German military spending had already reached 23% of GDP, even before its invasion of Poland in September 1939 and its subsequent commencement of actual military campaigns of invasion and occupation.

Not surprisingly, the same kind of claim on resources occurred when the United States took it upon itself to counter the aggression of Germany and Japan on a global basis. By 1944 defense spending had reason from 3% of GDP in the 1930s to 40% of America’s GDP, and would have totaled more than $2 trillion per year in present day dollars of purchasing power.

Military Spending As A Percent Of GDP In Nazi Germany

By contrast, during the final year before Washington/NATO triggered the Ukraine proxy war in February 2022, the Russian military budget was $65 billion, which amounted to just 3.5% of its GDP.

Moreover, the prior years showed no build-up of the kind that has always accompanied historic aggressors. For the period 1995 to 2022, for instance, the average military spending by Russia was 3.8% of GDP – with a minimum of 2.7% in 1998 and a maximum of 5.4% in 2016.

Needless to say, you don’t invade the Baltics or Poland – to say nothing of Germany, France, the Benelux and crossing the English Channel – on 3.5% of GDP! Not even remotely.

Since full scale war broke out in 2022 Russian military spending has increased significantly to 6% of GDP, but all of that is being consumed by the Demolition Derby in Ukraine – barely 100 miles from its own border.

That is, even at 6% of GDP Russia has not yet been able to subdue its own historic borderlands. So if Russia self-evidently does not have the economic and military capacity to conquer its own former borderlands, what is the war really about?

In short, it is rooted in the mess of peoples, borders, artifical polities and religious/ethnic/ language stew-pots left behind by the collapse or the Soviet Union in 1991. And the resulting territorial disputes and civil strife in these lands, which had been vassals or integral parts of greater Russia for several centuries, was no threat to the homeland security of America or anyone else.

At the end of the day, “Ukraine” actually means “borderlands” in the Russian language, connoting stateless areas that were first assembled into a coherent polity by Lenin, Stalin and Khrushchev by force of arms after 1920.

In fact, prior to the communist takeover of Russia, no country that even faintly resembled today’s Ukrainian borders had ever existed. So what NATO’s proxy war actually amounts to is an insensible attempt to enforce the dead hand of the Soviet presidium, as we amplify below.

For avoidance of doubt here are sequential maps that tell the story, and which make mincemeat of the Washington/NATO sanctity of borders malarkey. The first of these is a, where the yellow area depicts the approximate territory of the five regions – Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhia plus Crimea – that form the battle front of the war.

As it has happened, these regions have voted overwhelmingly during referendums in 2023 and 2014, respectively, to separate from Ukraine in favor of affiliation with Russia.

Collectively, the five regions were historically known as “Novorossiya” or “New Russia” and had been acquired by Russian rulers, including Catherine the Great between 1734 and 1791.

The red number markings within the yellow areas of the map designate the year of Russian acquisition. Self-evidently, therefore, the Russian Empire had gradually gained control over this vast area north of the Black Sea before the end of the 18th century. To that end, it had signed peace treaties with the Cossack Hetmanate (1734) and with the Ottoman Empire at the conclusion of the various Russo-Turkish Wars of that era.

Pursuant to this expansion drive – which included massive Russian investment and the in-migration of large Russian populations to the region – Russia established the “Novorossiysk Governaorate” in 1764. The latter was originally to be named after the Empress Catherine, but she decreed that it should be called “New Russia” instead.

The Provinces Of Ukraine Slated For Partition By The Trump Plan Were Part Of Russia Before The US Constitution Was Even Written

Completing the assemblage of New Russia, Catherine forcefully liquidated its aforementioned century-long Cossack ally known as the Zaporizhian Sich (present day Zaporizhia) in 1775 and annexed its territory to Novorossiya, thus eliminating the independent rule of the Ukrainian Cossacks. Later in 1783 she acquired Crimea from the Turks, which was also added to Novorossiya, as shown in yellow area of the map above.

During this formative period, the infamous shadow ruler under Catherine, Prince Grigori Potemkin, directed the sweeping settlement and Russification of these lands. Effectively, Catherine had granted him the powers of an absolute ruler over the area from 1774 onward.

The spirit and importance of “New Russia” at this time is aptly captured by the historian Willard Sunderland,

“The old steppe was Asian and stateless; the current one was state-determined and claimed for European-Russian civilization.

The adoption of the name of New Russia was in fact the most powerful statement imaginable of Russia’s national coming of age.

In fact, the passage of time solidified the borders of Novorossiya even more completely. One century later the light-yellow area of the below gave an unmistakable message: To wit, in the late Russian Empire there was no doubt as to the paternity of the lands adjacent to the Azov Sea and the Black Sea: They were now part of the 125 years-old “New Russia”.

After the Russian Revolution, of course, the pieces and parts in this region of the old Czarist Empire were bundled-up into a convenient administrative entity by the new red rulers of Moscow, who christened it the “Ukrainian SSR” (Soviet Socialist Republic). In a like manner, they created similar administrative entities in Belorussia, Georgia, Moldavia, Turkmenistan etc. – ultimately confecting 15 such faux “republics”.

During the course of this communist state-building, here is how and when these brutal tyrants attached each piece of today’s Ukrainian map to the territories acquired or seized by the Russian Czars over 1654-1917 (yellow area):

The old Novorossiya of the Donbas and Black Sea rim was added to the Ukraine SSR by Lenin in 1922.

Upon the death of the bloody Stalin in 1954, Khrushchev made a deal with his Presidium allies to transfer Crimea from the Russian SSR to the Ukrainian SSR in return for their support in the battle for succession.

In a word, Ukraine is the bastard spawn of communist blood and iron. Yet during the last decade the Washington and the NATO warhawks have spent upwards of $300 billion to ensure that the handiwork of autocratic Czars and Commissars remains intact into the 21st century and presumably beyond.

It is ironic, therefore, that the historically illiterate Donald Trump has the good sense to now attempt to dispense with one of the stupidest crusades that the War Party on the Potomac has yet concocted. So doing, he might actually enable the failed handiwork of communist tyrants to be made right with history – an outcome that can now happen if and only if the Donald finally makes a partition deal with Putin.

Under this benign counterfactual, they would have presumably combined peoples of like ethnic, linguistic, religious and politico-cultural history into a cohesive natural polity and state. Not surprisingly, therefore, virtually from the minute it came out from under the communist yoke when the Soviet Union was swept into the dustbin of history in 1991, Ukraine has been engulfed in political and actual civil war. The elections which did occur were essentially 50/50 at the national level but reflected dueling 80/20 vote breakouts within the regions. That is, the Ukrainian nationalist candidates tended to get vote margins of 80% + in the West/Central areas, while Russian-sympathizing candidates got similar pluralities in the mainly Russian-speaking East and South.

This pattern transpired because once the iron-hand of totalitarian rule ended in 1991, the deep and historically rooted conflict between Ukrainian nationalism, language and politics of the central and western regions of the country and the Russian language and historical religious and political affinities of the Donbas and south came rushing to the surface.

Accordingly, so-called democracy barely survived these contests until February 2014 when one of Washington’s “color revolutions” finally “succeeded”. That is to say, the Washington fomented and financed nationalist-led coupe d état ended the fragile post-communist equilibrium.

That’s the true meaning of the Maidan coup. It ended the tenuous cohesion that kept the artificial state of Ukraine intact for barely two decades after the Soviet demise. So save for Washington’s destructive intervention, the partition of a communist-confected state that had never been built to last would have materialized all on its own – perhaps like in Czechoslovakia – and likely sooner than later.

At the end of the day, therefore, the necessary impending partition of the rogue state of Ukraine is not a case at all of legitimate sovereign borders being violated. Nor does it involve an assault on the hypocritical notion of a “rules-based international order” that has not actually ever existed and which, instead, has been a cover for Washington’s global hegemony all along.

But the lessons are nonetheless profound. History accumulates and eventually leads to destructive, but wholly unnecessary outcomes.

That is the case today with the utterly foolish action of Washington during the 1990s and 2000s to bring former Warsaw Pact Nations, and even breakaway Soviet Republics into a NATO alliance whose mission was over and done in 1991.

It should have been dismantled then and there. When the old Soviet monster with its 50,000 tanks and 7,000 nuclear warheads disappeared into the dustbin of history, there was no longer a threat to the east. There was no “front line” to defend.
